findings.attack_scenario:
An attacker holds a staff refresh token (localStorage exfil via XSS, a shared machine, a stolen laptop). The victim notices and does the one thing the product offers: /auth/forgot-password then /auth/set-password.

auth.py:197 rewrites hashed_password and auth.py:202 issues a new refresh token — but nothing deletes the attacker's row from refresh_tokens. The DELETE that change_password performs at auth.py:243-245 has no counterpart on this path. The attacker POSTs their old token to /auth/refresh; _consume_refresh_token (auth.py:78-120) finds the row, sees revoked_at IS NULL and expires_at up to 14 days out, and mints a fresh access token plus a fresh refresh token. They ride that rotation chain indefinitely.

The password reset — the only remediation available to the victim — accomplishes nothing. Any access token minted before the reset also stays valid for its full 60 minutes: there is no jti and no denylist anywhere in the codebase. users.py deactivate_user (users.py:196) and anonymize_me (users.py:72) have the same gap.
findings.remediation:
Delete the user's refresh tokens before issuing the new pair, matching change_password:

    db.add(user)
    db.query(models.RefreshToken).filter(
        models.RefreshToken.user_id == user.id
    ).delete()
    db.flush()
    access_token = create_access_token({"sub": str(user.id), "role": user.role.value})
    raw_refresh = _issue_refresh_token(db, user)

Do the same in deactivate_user and anonymize_me. For access tokens, add `users.tokens_valid_after`, stamp `iat` on mint, and reject in get_current_user any token whose iat predates it — that closes the 60-minute residual window and pairs with BASE-SEC-01 (is_active never checked).

--- FIXED 2026-08-09. /auth/set-password now deletes the user's refresh tokens before issuing the new pair (routers/auth.py), matching change_password. Regression test: test_set_password_revokes_every_existing_refresh_token.

findings.title: Refresh-token rotation has no reuse detection — a replayed token 401s but never kills the family
findings.vulnerable_code:
if (
        rt is None
        or rt.revoked_at is not None
        or rt.expires_at < datetime.now(timezone.utc)
    ):
        raise HTTPException(
            status_code=status.HTTP_401_UNAUTHORIZED,
            detail={"code": "AUTH_REFRESH_INVALID", ...},
        )
    ...
    # Delete (rotate) the consumed token so it cannot be replayed
    db.delete(rt)
findings.attack_scenario:
Rotation is implemented (the row is deleted at auth.py:118, so a token cannot be used twice) but the security signal it produces is discarded.

An attacker steals refresh token R1 and uses it first. auth.py:118 deletes the R1 row and auth.py:346 issues R2 to the attacker. The victim's browser later presents R1; the row is gone, so auth.py:94 takes the `rt is None` branch and returns a flat 401 — indistinguishable from an expired token or a typo. Because the row was deleted rather than retained-and-marked, and because there is no family/lineage id linking R1 to R2, the server cannot tell 'stolen-token replay' from 'stale tab'. Nothing revokes R2.

The victim's client logs them out; they log in again, creating an additional independent token row and leaving the attacker's chain untouched. Detecting exactly this is the reason refresh rotation exists.
findings.remediation:
Retain consumed rows and add a family id so replay is both detectable and lethal:

# models.py RefreshToken
    family_id = Column(UUID(as_uuid=True), nullable=False, index=True)
    consumed_at = Column(DateTime(timezone=True), nullable=True)

# auth.py _consume_refresh_token — replace `db.delete(rt)`
    if rt.consumed_at is not None:
        db.query(models.RefreshToken).filter(
            models.RefreshToken.family_id == rt.family_id
        ).update({"revoked_at": datetime.now(timezone.utc)})
        db.commit()
        raise HTTPException(401, detail={"code": "AUTH_REFRESH_REUSE"})
    rt.consumed_at = datetime.now(timezone.utc)

Carry family_id through _issue_refresh_token, and delete the dead duplicate implementation at deps.py:254-285 so a future caller cannot pick the weaker one.
findings.remediation_applied: RefreshToken gains family_id + consumed_at (migration 0040). Rotation marks consumed instead of deleting; replay of a consumed token revokes the whole family, logs refresh_token_reuse_detected and returns AUTH_REFRESH_REUSE. Test updated: tests/test_auth.py::test_refresh_rotates_token

findings.title: get_event_schedule is organizer-callable with no owner check, and it hands out the slot_ids and shift_ids the write tools consume
findings.attack_scenario:
_schedule_handler binds `scope` and never reads it — there is no `if not scope.see_all and event.owner_id != scope.module_owner_id` guard, unlike get_module_roster.py:51, which has exactly that line against the same Event table.

An organizer supplies any event id belonging to another organizer. Event ids are not secret: they appear in URLs, in prior conversation history, in move_participant arguments, and in copilot_tool_calls.args_json. The handler returns the other organizer's title, school, `location` (the room), visibility, module_slug, date range, a live signup headcount (events_edit.py:204), every orientation slot with room and capacity, and every shift_id / slot_id.

Those ids are the documented inputs to reschedule_slot (events_edit.py:500, admin+organizer) and mark_attendance / move_volunteer_to_shift (operations.py:264, 414). So this read gap is also the id-discovery step that makes the write-scoping gap (BASE-SEC-03) reachable in practice rather than theoretically.
findings.remediation_applied: Covered by the same deny_if_not_owned guard on _schedule_handler.

findings.title: DELETE /events/{id} cascade-destroys every signup, shift commitment and attendance record for the event, with no guard
findings.vulnerable_code:
ensure_event_staff_access(event, current_user)
    quarter_service.ensure_event_quarter_writable(event)

    db.delete(event)
    db.commit()

# models.py:276 / 279 / 404 / 347 / 527 — the cascade chain
    slots = relationship("Slot", back_populates="event", cascade="all, delete-orphan")
    shifts = relationship("Shift", back_populates="event", cascade="all, delete-orphan", ...)
    signups = relationship("Signup", back_populates="slot", cascade="all, delete-orphan")
    shift_signups = relationship("ShiftSignup", back_populates="shift", cascade="all, delete-orphan")
    session_attendance = relationship("SessionAttendance", back_populates="shift_signup", cascade="all, delete-orphan")
findings.attack_scenario:
Any organizer (ensure_event_staff_access is role-based, not ownership-based) can DELETE a finished event to tidy up. db.delete(event) triggers the full ORM cascade: Event→slots→signups and session_attendance; Event→shifts→shift_signups→session_attendance. Every attended/no_show record, every SignupResponse and every SentNotification row for that event is physically deleted.

Volunteer-hours and attendance-rate analytics (admin.py:1559, 1612) silently lose that quarter's history, and orientation credit granted from attendance can no longer be justified from the record. The only trace left is one `event_delete` AuditLog row naming an id that no longer resolves — and per BASE-QUAL-13 even that row is discarded, because log_action runs after db.commit() here.

The sibling path already knows better: DELETE /shifts/{id} calls shift_service.ensure_no_active_signups (shifts.py:127) before deleting.
findings.remediation:
Refuse to hard-delete an event that has booking history, mirroring the shift path:

    has_bookings = (
        db.query(models.Signup.id).join(models.Slot, models.Slot.id == models.Signup.slot_id)
          .filter(models.Slot.event_id == event.id).first()
        or db.query(models.ShiftSignup.id).join(models.Shift, models.Shift.id == models.ShiftSignup.shift_id)
          .filter(models.Shift.event_id == event.id).first()
    )
    if has_bookings:
        raise HTTPException(409, detail="Event has signup history; archive it instead of deleting.")

Better: give Event a `deleted_at` soft-delete column (Module already has one, models.py:845) and reserve hard delete for events with zero bookings.

findings.title: No pgvector HNSW index is created by any migration — a fresh deploy leaves every copilot retrieval on a sequential scan
findings.vulnerable_code:
sa.Column("embedding", Vector(1024), nullable=False),
...
    # 5. Indexes (no HNSW on embedding — that lands in plan 04 via
    # the ingest CLI's --build-index flag; building HNSW pre-bulk-load is
    # materially slower per-row. See RESEARCH D8 / Pitfall 5.).
findings.attack_scenario:
The HNSW index exists only as an application function: corpus/ingest.py:464-482 builds `ix_corpus_chunks_embedding_hnsw ON corpus_chunks USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops) WITH (m=16, ef_construction=64)`, reachable only via the `--build-index` CLI flag (corpus/__main__.py:97,121).

The docker migrate service runs `alembic upgrade head && python -m app.seed_admin` (docker-compose.yml:65) — it never invokes the ingest CLI. So a freshly deployed production database has the vector column and no vector index. Every copilot retrieval does a full sequential scan computing 1024-dimension cosine distance per row. At the documented ~4,731-chunk corpus (0020 docstring) that is roughly 5M float ops per query, on every single copilot turn, degrading linearly as the corpus grows.

Nothing in the deploy path will ever fix it — the deferral was deliberate and correct for bulk-load performance, but the follow-up step was never wired into deployment.
findings.remediation:
Add the index build to the deploy sequence, after ingestion (HNSW on an empty table is useless):

  alembic upgrade head && python -m app.seed_admin && python -m app.corpus --build-index

or add a final migration issuing `CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS ix_corpus_chunks_embedding_hnsw ON corpus_chunks USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops) WITH (m=16, ef_construction=64)`.

Verify post-deploy: `SELECT indexname FROM pg_indexes WHERE tablename='corpus_chunks';` and confirm an `EXPLAIN` on a retrieval query shows an Index Scan rather than a Seq Scan.
findings.remediation_applied: Migration 0039 creates the HNSW index on corpus_chunks.embedding, guarded on the table and the pgvector opclass existing.

findings.title: The two hottest foreign keys in the schema are unindexed: slots.event_id and signups.slot_id
findings.vulnerable_code:
event_id = Column(UUID(as_uuid=True), ForeignKey("events.id"), nullable=False)
...
    __table_args__ = (
        Index("ix_slots_start_time", "start_time"),
        Index("ix_slots_shift_id_sort_order", "shift_id", "sort_order"),
    )

# signups — the only index is a UNIQUE whose LEADING column is volunteer_id
    slot_id = Column(UUID(as_uuid=True), ForeignKey("slots.id"), nullable=False)
    __table_args__ = (
        UniqueConstraint("volunteer_id", "slot_id", name="uq_signups_volunteer_id_slot_id"),
    )
findings.attack_scenario:
Cross-referenced against the full index inventory of all 39 migrations. The only indexes ever created on `slots` are ix_slots_start_time (0002:114) and ix_slots_shift_id_sort_order (0037:211). There is no index on event_id anywhere.

Every event-detail page, roster load and shift listing joins slots on event_id — each one is a full sequential scan of the table, and slots are never deleted, so the cost grows monotonically across quarters.

signups is worse-disguised: uq_signups_volunteer_id_slot_id backs an index on (volunteer_id, slot_id), which Postgres cannot use for a `WHERE slot_id = ?` predicate because slot_id is not the leading column. Every 'who signed up for this slot' query — organizer roster, check-in screen, capacity count — seq-scans signups. `signups.status` is likewise unindexed and is the filter in the 0029 and 0033 backfills.
findings.remediation:
One short migration:

    op.create_index("ix_slots_event_id", "slots", ["event_id"])
    op.create_index("ix_signups_slot_id_status", "signups", ["slot_id", "status"])

The composite covers both the FK lookup and the status filter. Tables are small enough today that a plain (non-CONCURRENT) create is fine — do it before they grow. Confirm with EXPLAIN on the roster query before and after.
findings.remediation_applied: Migration 0039 adds ix_slots_event_id and ix_signups_slot_id_status. shift_signups already had its index from 0037 — the audit finding was wrong on that third one.

findings.title: Per-IP rate limiting reads request.client.host with no proxy-header handling — behind a load balancer the entire public surface shares one bucket
findings.vulnerable_code:
key = f"rate:{request.client.host}:{request.url.path}"
        current = redis_client.incr(key)
...
# Dockerfile:27 — no --proxy-headers, no --forwarded-allow-ips
CMD ["uvicorn", "app.main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]
findings.attack_scenario:
Deployed behind any TLS-terminating proxy, ALB or ingress — which the production topology assumes — request.client.host is the proxy's address for every request. The Redis key `rate:<proxy-ip>:/api/v1/public/signups` becomes a single global counter.

One client issuing 11 signup POSTs in 60 seconds (routers/public/signups.py:40, max_requests=10) then returns 429 to every volunteer worldwide for the remainder of the window. Normal traffic from a lecture hall behind campus NAT does this accidentally. /public/orientation-check collapses at 5/60 (routers/public/orientation.py:30).

The inverse failure matters too: if the deployment DOES enable --proxy-headers without an allow-list of trusted proxy IPs, any client can spoof X-Forwarded-For and evade the limiter entirely. Both halves need to be got right at once.
findings.remediation:
Run uvicorn with `--proxy-headers --forwarded-allow-ips=<trusted proxy CIDR>` (never `*` on a publicly reachable port), so request.client.host is the real client.

Then stop relying on IP alone for the signup path — add a per-email counter alongside the per-IP one, the way magic_link_service.check_rate_limit already does (magic_link_service.py:366-383, which correctly hashes the address before keying Redis).
findings.remediation_applied: Addressed together with BASE-CONFIG-27: with XFF overwritten at the edge and trust narrowed, request.client.host is the real client. Rate limiter also handles request.client being None.

findings.title: Sentry is initialised with no request-body scrubbing — a 500 on /auth/change-password ships plaintext passwords to a third party
findings.vulnerable_code:
sentry_sdk.init(
        dsn=settings.sentry_dsn,
        environment=settings.environment,
        # Error monitoring only — no performance tracing volume.
        traces_sample_rate=0.0,
    )
findings.attack_scenario:
send_default_pii is correctly left at its default False, so cookies and the Authorization header are stripped. But max_request_body_size defaults to "medium" and the ASGI extractor attaches the parsed JSON body independently of the PII flag — nothing here overrides it, and there is no before_send hook.

An unhandled exception inside POST /auth/change-password (auth.py:218-248, body {current_password, new_password}) — a DB blip at auth.py:247 is enough — is captured with both plaintext passwords in event.request.data. The same applies to POST /auth/set-password (auth.py:146-149, carrying a live invite/reset JWT, which per BASE-SEC-22 is itself an admin bearer credential) and POST /auth/refresh (auth.py:127-128).

Anyone with access to the Sentry project — a third party outside the application's trust boundary — then holds working credentials.
findings.remediation_applied: Sentry init now sets send_default_pii=False, max_request_body_size='never' and a before_send scrubber dropping request data, cookies and auth headers.

findings.title: weekly_digest mails every volunteer with no dedup, no daily-limit check, no retry policy and no time limit
findings.attack_scenario:
weekly_digest is the only mail task with no sent_notifications dedup claim — compare send_reminders_24h (celery_app.py:459 `if _dedup_insert(db, s.id, "reminder_24h")`) and send_broadcast (broadcast_service.py:446).

RedBeat can fire a schedule twice: lock churn on restart, two beat containers during a rolling deploy, or a worker requeue (task_acks_late=True and task_reject_on_worker_lost=True are both set at celery_app.py:50-51). Nothing in the task body detects a second run, so every volunteer with a booking in the next 7 days receives the digest again.

Two compounding defects in the same function: the loop never calls _check_daily_send_limit (which exists at celery_app.py:271 and 610 but not here), so a double send is also invisible to the provider circuit breaker and can starve the day's transactional confirmations; and the plain @celery.task decorator means a mid-loop SMTP failure aborts the run with no retry and no dead-letter, so every volunteer after the failure point silently gets nothing. The DB session opened at line 526 is held across the entire serial SMTP fan-out.
findings.remediation_applied: weekly_digest is now bound with autoretry_for/retry_backoff/max_retries=3/time_limit=600/soft_time_limit=540, checks _check_daily_send_limit, and claims a per-volunteer per-ISO-week dedup row before sending.

findings.title: log_action is called after db.commit() in eight mutating endpoints, so those audit rows are silently discarded
findings.vulnerable_code:
# events.py:327-329 — commit first, log after
    db.delete(event)
    db.commit()

    log_action(db, current_user, "event_delete", "Event", str(event.id))

# deps.py:300-302 — the helper's stated contract
    Add an audit log entry to the current transaction.
    IMPORTANT: no commit here. Caller controls commit/rollback.

# database.py:26-31 — what happens to the pending INSERT
def get_db():
    db = SessionLocal()
    try:
        yield db
    finally:
        db.close()
findings.attack_scenario:
VERIFIED by grep: in events.py every log_action line number is greater than its preceding db.commit(); same in slots.py at 149/152, 245/248, 288/290.

log_action only db.add()s an AuditLog to the session (deps.py:292-312, no commit by design). When it runs after the commit, the session is clean and nothing commits afterwards, so get_db's `finally: db.close()` discards the INSERT.

Result: event create, event update, event delete, slot generation, and slot create/update/delete produce NO audit record at all — the post-incident trail is empty for precisely the destructive staff actions, including the cascade delete in BASE-SEC-27. Other call sites get the ordering right (signups.py:110-112, organizer.py:100-115), which is what makes this a slip rather than a design choice. Same family as BASE-SEC-13 (seven uncommitted log_action calls in admin.py).
findings.remediation:
Move each log_action above its commit:

    log_action(db, current_user, "event_delete", "Event", str(event.id))
    db.delete(event)
    db.commit()

Then add one regression test per mutating endpoint asserting an audit_logs row exists after the call — the reason this survived is that nothing asserts on the trail.

findings.title: Tool pii_schema is declared on all 34 copilot tools and read by no code — the allow-list is documentation, not a control
findings.attack_scenario:
grep for `pii_schema` across backend/app/ returns only the field declaration at base.py:16 and the 34 `pii_schema=_..._SCHEMA` keyword arguments. No dispatcher, no boundary layer, no test harness ever reads the attribute. _complete passes the raw handler result straight to scrub.

The only field filtering that actually happens is each handler voluntarily calling schema_apply() on itself, with the same module-level list it also passed to pii_schema — so declaration and enforcement can never disagree, and equally the declaration proves nothing.

Live consequence: quarters._list_handler (quarters.py:79-84) returns {"quarters": [...], "count": ...} with no schema_apply on the outer dict at all, and nothing notices. A tool added tomorrow that forgets the schema_apply line returns its ORM row wholesale, with only the redactor's four regexes between the database and OpenRouter — and names, staff notes and free-text prose match none of them (BASE-SEC-31).
findings.remediation:
Enforce the declaration at the single dispatch point rather than trusting 34 handlers:

# base.py::_complete
    raw = tool.handler(db, scope, args)
    if not (isinstance(raw, dict) and "error" in raw):
        raw = schema_apply(raw, allowed_fields=tool.pii_schema)
    scrubbed, events = scrub(raw, declared=True)

Apply the same two lines in confirmation.py::execute_after_confirmation (line 170) so the confirmed-write path is covered. The per-handler schema_apply calls then become defence in depth. This change forces the pii_schema lists to be made complete — several are currently missing their own top-level keys (list_modules declares id/name/week/school but returns {"modules": [...]}), which is exactly the audit worth doing.

findings.title: schema_filter passes an entire nested subtree whenever the parent key is declared without a dotted rule
findings.attack_scenario:
The module docstring promises 'Deny-by-default.' That holds at the top level only. `nested` is built solely from field strings containing a '.' (schema_filter.py:18-21); a declared key with no dotted rule falls to `else: out[key] = value` and its entire subtree is copied verbatim, however deep.

_CREDIT_SCHEMA declares a bare "credits" (orientation_credits.py:49) over holder dicts; _STAFF_SCHEMA a bare "staff" (staff.py:41); _TEMPLATE_SCHEMA a bare "templates" (module_templates.py:52); _EVENT_SCHEMA a bare "shifts" (events_edit.py:66). Those row builders are clean today — the failure mode is the next edit. Adding `"email": v.email` to the holder dict produces no filter error and no test failure; it is caught only by the redactor's email regex. Adding `"phone": v.phone_e164` or a guardian name would not be caught at all.

Contrast get_module_roster.py:34-41, which uses dotted `participants.*` rules and therefore genuinely drops the email and phone it selects at lines 73-74. The mechanism works; it is just not applied where it matters most.

findings.title: declared=True is hardcoded on every copilot tool path, so the redactor's HIGH-severity boundary-bug alarm can never fire
findings.vulnerable_code:
raw = tool.handler(db, scope, args)
    scrubbed, events = scrub(raw, declared=True)
...
            scrubbed, events = scrub(objection, declared=True)
...
# confirmation.py:171
    scrubbed, events = scrub(raw, declared=True)

# redactor.py:47 — the severity that is now unreachable
    severity = "LOW" if declared else "HIGH"
findings.attack_scenario:
redactor.py:8-12 states the contract: 'A hit on an undeclared payload means schema-filter and role-scope both let the value through — this is a boundary bug upstream and is flagged HIGH.'

All three production call sites that scrub tool output pass declared=True unconditionally. The only declared=False caller in the backend is memory/extractor.py:152, an unrelated path.

So if a handler ever forgets schema_apply and leaks an email — precisely the layer-1 failure the HIGH severity exists to announce — the redactor rewrites it, records it as LOW, and update_status stores only `redactions_applied = <int>` (audit_log.py:81, 94). No severity is persisted, no alert fires, and the count is indistinguishable from a roster whose names happened to contain an @-sign. The layer-3 backstop works; the detector attached to it does not. This is what makes BASE-SEC-28 and BASE-SEC-29 silent rather than noisy.
findings.remediation:
Derive `declared` from what was actually permitted instead of hardcoding it. Once pii_schema is enforced (BASE-SEC-28), scrub the dropped remainder in strict mode and alert on any hit:

    filtered = schema_apply(raw, allowed_fields=tool.pii_schema)
    scrubbed, events = scrub(filtered, declared=True)
    _, leaked = scrub(_dropped_by(raw, filtered), declared=False)
    if leaked:
        logger.error("copilot_boundary_leak tool=%s kinds=%s",
                     tool.name, sorted({e.kind for e in leaked}))

and persist max(e.severity for e in events) alongside redactions_applied in audit_log.update_status so a HIGH is queryable after the fact.

findings.title: Volunteer full names and free-text staff notes cross the boundary to the model provider, and the system prompt says nothing about handling them
findings.vulnerable_code:
You are speaking with an admin. Admins manage quarters, modules,
orientation credits, staff accounts, exports, audit logs, and
global settings, and can act on any event. They can see everything in
the UI; you don't need to over-redact your explanations.
findings.attack_scenario:
The boundary's entire PII posture is four regexes (redactor.py:31-40): email, dashed SSN, NANP phone, UCSB NID. Names match none of them and are explicitly permitted by the schema filter (participants.name, get_module_roster.py:38).

_complete scrubs the roster, then loop.py:324-330 serialises it into a role:tool message and adapter.py:142 posts the transcript to OpenRouter — on every subsequent turn, since the message stays in `messages`. What travels: every volunteer's full first+last name on a roster (get_module_roster.py:67, participant_history.py:67, orientation_credits.py:200), OrientationCredit.notes free text written by staff (orientation_credits.py:262), and event location/description. The summariser shares the same adapter, so rosters also land in compressed conversation state.

Nothing in the system prompt addresses data handling: rules 1-11 cover tool grounding, confirmation cards, timezone, terseness and dates. The only sentence touching the subject points the wrong way — 'you don't need to over-redact your explanations.'
findings.remediation:
Two changes. Add a data-handling rule to _AGENT_EXTRA_RULES (prompts.py:91) and bump SYSTEM_PROMPT_VERSION (line 19) as the module's own versioning rule requires:

  12. Tool results may contain volunteers' names and staff notes. Use them to
      answer the question that was asked and no further: do not list a roster
      the user did not ask for, do not repeat a name into a summary, and never
      copy a free-text note verbatim — say what it means instead.

And reword the _ADMIN_TAIL clause, which is about UI visibility but reads to the model as licence to restate personal data: 'Admins can see everything in the UI, so explain features fully — that is not licence to restate personal data the question did not need.'

findings.title: The manage magic-link token is a permanent, unrevocable bearer credential in a URL that discloses a volunteer's identity and full schedule
findings.vulnerable_code:
# 2026-07-28 spec: expires_at is the CONFIRMATION deadline only.
    # Manage stays usable for as long as the token row exists (rows die
    # with their signup via cascade, or via the stale-token sweep).
    token_row = _lookup_token(db, token)
    if token_row is None:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=400, detail="token invalid")
    if token_row.purpose not in MANAGE_PURPOSES:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=400, detail="token not valid for manage")
findings.attack_scenario:
The token travels in a query string (GET /public/signups/manage?token=...), so it lands in browser history, proxy and access logs, and forwarded email.

manage_signups never checks expires_at and never checks consumed_at (public/signups.py:126-131) — a token the volunteer already burned on /public/signups/confirm still works, indefinitely, for anyone holding the string. Anyone who obtains it reads the volunteer's full first and last name, their event, every session and shift they hold, and their waitlist positions (public/signups.py:221-229).

Until expires_at they can additionally read the phone number and flip reminder/SMS settings via /public/preferences — which DOES enforce expiry (preferences.py:28). The two endpoints disagree about the lifetime of the same token, which is the clearest sign the unbounded lifetime was not a considered decision. There is no revocation endpoint anywhere in the routers.
findings.remediation:
Give manage access a bounded lifetime and a revocation path:

    # public/signups.py, mirroring preferences.py:28
    if token_row.expires_at < datetime.now(timezone.utc):

findings.title: Audit-log export is a 2N+ query N+1 — up to ~20,000 sequential SELECTs in a single synchronous request
findings.attack_scenario:
GET /admin/audit-logs.csv loads up to 10,000 rows in one shot (admin.py:1525) and calls humanize(log, db) per row (admin.py:1535).

Each call fires one User query in _resolve_actor plus one entity query in _resolve_entity, and the Signup/ShiftSignup branches then lazy-load .volunteer, .slot and .slot.event (audit_log_humanize.py:125-139, 158-163) for several more round-trips each.

The paginated list endpoint has the same shape at page_size up to 500.

Add joinedload for Signup.volunteer, Signup.slot and Slot.event on the batched query, and cap the CSV export by date range rather than by a flat 10,000-row limit.

findings.title: refresh_tokens grows without bound — no expiry reaper, no per-user session cap, no way to list live sessions
findings.vulnerable_code:
class RefreshToken(Base):
    __tablename__ = "refresh_tokens"

    id = Column(UUID(as_uuid=True), primary_key=True, default=uuid.uuid4)
    user_id = Column(UUID(as_uuid=True), ForeignKey("users.id"), nullable=False)
    token_hash = Column(String(512), unique=True, index=True, nullable=False)
    created_at = Column(DateTime(timezone=True), default=lambda: datetime.now(timezone.utc))
    expires_at = Column(DateTime(timezone=True), nullable=False)
    revoked_at = Column(DateTime(timezone=True), nullable=True)
findings.attack_scenario:
The full beat_schedule is weekly-digest, expire-pending-signups, archive-ended-quarters, check-reminders and copilot-sweep-idle-sessions — nothing reaps refresh_tokens, and there is no cleanup in app/tasks/. Rows are removed only by the rotation delete at auth.py:118 and the bulk delete at auth.py:243.

So: every logout leaves a permanent revoked row; every login and every SSO callback adds a row with no cap on concurrent live sessions per user; and rows belonging to deleted or deactivated users remain live and usable (which is BASE-SEC-01's persistence layer).

An attacker holding a password can accumulate unlimited independent 14-day sessions, and neither the admin UI nor any endpoint lists a user's live sessions — so the accumulation is invisible to the people who would need to notice it. The table only grows, and every /auth/refresh scans an index that only gets larger.
findings.remediation:
Add a reaper and a cap:

    @celery.task(name="app.tasks.cleanup.reap_refresh_tokens")
    def reap_refresh_tokens():
        with SessionLocal() as db:
            now = datetime.now(timezone.utc)
            db.query(models.RefreshToken).filter(
                or_(models.RefreshToken.expires_at < now,
                    models.RefreshToken.revoked_at < now - timedelta(days=7))
            ).delete(synchronize_session=False)
            db.commit()

findings.title: Access and refresh tokens are both stored in localStorage, so one XSS yields a 14-day renewable session
findings.attack_scenario:
localStorage is readable by any JavaScript running on the origin, and unlike an HttpOnly cookie there is no browser-level protection. Any XSS anywhere in the SPA — a dependency compromise, a future component that renders user-supplied HTML, a malicious browser extension — exfiltrates both tokens with two getItem calls.

The access token alone would be a 60-minute problem. Storing the REFRESH token beside it makes the compromise durable: the attacker replays it against POST /auth/refresh and rotates indefinitely (14-day expiry, auth.py:56). Because rotation has no reuse detection (BASE-SEC-25), the victim's own client hitting the rotated-away token just gets a flat 401 and logs them out — the theft is indistinguishable from a stale tab.

Until this session's fix, a password reset did not evict that token either (BASE-SEC-24), so the victim had no remedy at all. That half is now closed; the storage exposure is not.
findings.remediation:
Move the refresh token to an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Strict cookie scoped to /api/v1/auth/refresh, so JavaScript cannot read it and the browser attaches it only to the refresh call:

    response.set_cookie("uvse_refresh", raw_refresh, httponly=True, secure=True,
                        samesite="strict", path="/api/v1/auth/refresh",
                        max_age=14 * 24 * 3600)

Keep the short-lived access token in memory (a module variable) rather than localStorage — it is then lost on reload, which the refresh cookie transparently repairs. This requires CORS credentials handling, so pair it with the CORS review in BASE-CONFIG-05.

--- ACCEPTED RISK 2026-08-12 (Andy's call, after the trade was explained). Moving refresh tokens to httpOnly cookies is the correct fix and is not a small change: it means a cookie-based refresh endpoint, CSRF protection on it, and a rework of how the SPA authenticates every call — days of work touching the one subsystem whose breakage locks all staff out. The exposure it removes only materialises if an XSS lands first, and the app has no user-supplied HTML rendering path. Revisit if a CSP is added (the cheaper first move against the same threat) or if any rich-text/HTML-rendering feature is introduced, which would change the likelihood of the precondition.

findings.title: The SPA is served with no security headers at all — the app's own CSP applies only to API responses
findings.exact_lines: 4-25 (entire server block); compare backend/app/main.py:88-101 and Caddyfile:15
findings.attack_scenario:
The backend middleware at main.py:88-101 sets X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options, Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy and a CSP — but those headers ride on JSON API responses, where they do almost nothing. The document that actually executes JavaScript is index.html, served by this nginx block, and it carries none of them. Caddy adds only Strict-Transport-Security (Caddyfile:15).

Consequences on the real HTML document: no CSP, so an injected script from any origin executes and can read the tokens in localStorage (BASE-SEC-41) — CSP is the main mitigation that would blunt an XSS into a non-event. No X-Frame-Options/frame-ancestors, so the admin UI can be iframed by any site for clickjacking. No Referrer-Policy, so full URLs leak to third-party hosts on outbound navigation — and the set-password and manage-signup routes carry credentials in the query string (BASE-SEC-22, BASE-SEC-32). No X-Content-Type-Options, so a MIME-sniffed upload or asset can be executed as script.

This is the single highest-leverage config change available: it is one nginx block and it hardens every page at once.
findings.remediation_applied: frontend/nginx.conf now sets CSP, X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options, Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy and server_tokens off; Cache-Control moved to a map so no location block suppresses header inheritance.

findings.title: Production runs uvicorn with --forwarded-allow-ips=*, so any client can forge X-Forwarded-For and mint unlimited rate-limit buckets
findings.vulnerable_code:
# --proxy-headers: trust X-Forwarded-For from Caddy so the per-IP rate
    # limiter keys on the real client, not Caddy's network IP. Trusting all
    # proxies is safe here because port 8000 is never published — only Caddy
    # can reach the backend on the compose network.
    command: uvicorn app.main:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 --workers 4 --proxy-headers --forwarded-allow-ips=*
findings.attack_scenario:
VERIFIED against the uvicorn source (middleware/proxy_headers.py). With --forwarded-allow-ips=*, _TrustedHosts.always_trust is True, and get_trusted_client_host returns `x_forwarded_for_hosts[0]` — the LEFTMOST value in the header.

Caddy's reverse_proxy APPENDS the real client IP to any inbound X-Forwarded-For rather than replacing it. So a request arriving with `X-Forwarded-For: 9.9.9.9` reaches uvicorn as `9.9.9.9, <real client>`, and uvicorn takes 9.9.9.9 — a fully attacker-chosen value.

deps.py:58 then builds the Redis key as `rate:9.9.9.9:/api/v1/public/signups`. Incrementing a header integer per request gives a fresh bucket every time, so every per-IP limit in the app is bypassed: the 10/min signup cap, the 5/min orientation-credit probe (BASE-SEC-35), the 30/min login limiter, and the venue-code check-in path (BASE-SEC-05, a 4-digit code with no lockout — unlimited attempts means it falls in minutes).

The comment's reasoning is sound about WHO can open a TCP connection to port 8000, but the threat is the HEADER a public client sends THROUGH Caddy, which the network isolation does not touch.
findings.remediation_applied: --forwarded-allow-ips narrowed from * to 172.16.0.0/12, and Caddy now overwrites X-Forwarded-For with {remote_host} instead of appending.

findings.title: Logging out is client-side only — the refresh token stays valid on the server for its full 14 days
findings.exact_lines: 214-216; no counterpart endpoint exists in backend/app/routers/auth.py
findings.attack_scenario:
logout() deletes the two localStorage keys and nothing else. It makes no HTTP call, and grep of backend/app/routers/auth.py shows no /auth/logout or revoke endpoint to call — so the refresh_tokens row survives untouched with revoked_at NULL and expires_at up to 14 days out.

Anyone who captured the token before logout — shared or lab machine, browser sync to a personal device, an earlier XSS, a backup of the profile directory — keeps a working, self-renewing session long after the user believes they ended it. On the shared-workstation case that SciTrek plausibly has, "log out when you're done" is the instruction users are given, and it does not do what they are told it does.

It also means the refresh_tokens table only ever grows (BASE-QUAL-20): logout leaves the row behind rather than revoking it.

findings.title: No request has a timeout: every fetch in the API client can hang indefinitely
findings.exact_lines: 100, 121, 159-166, 194-199 (no AbortController or signal anywhere in the file)
findings.attack_scenario:
fetch has no default timeout. No call site constructs an AbortController or passes a signal, so any request whose response never arrives — a wedged worker thread, a dropped connection a proxy does not reset, a Postgres query with no statement_timeout (BASE-CONFIG-01) — leaves the promise pending forever.

The UI sits on its loading spinner with no error and no retry, because the catch block is never reached. Reloading is the user's only recourse, and reloading loses whatever form state they had. The paths where this hurts most are the slow ones the audit already flagged: the audit-log CSV export (BASE-CONFIG-24, tens of thousands of sequential queries) and the reminders preview (BASE-CONFIG-25).

The backend has the mirror-image gap — no statement_timeout and no request timeout — so nothing on either side bounds the wait.

findings.title: CSV and calendar downloads have no refresh-on-401, so every export fails once the access token is an hour old

findings.attack_scenario:
request() handles an expired access token by refreshing and retrying (api.js:106-127). downloadBlob duplicates the fetch logic without that block, so a 401 falls straight into the error branch.

Access tokens last 60 minutes. An admin who has had the tab open longer than that clicks Export and gets the raw string "GET /admin/audit-logs.csv failed (401)" — no refresh attempt, no re-login prompt, and no indication that simply reloading would fix it. Every download path is affected: the audit-log CSV, roster exports, and the .ics calendar files.

It is also silent in testing, because tests exercise downloads with a freshly minted token.

    restart: unless-stopped
findings.attack_scenario:
No service declares mem_limit, cpus, cap_drop, security_opt, read_only or pids_limit. On a single VPS — which the file's own header says is the deployment target — every container can consume the whole host.

Concrete failure paths already identified elsewhere in this audit: the copilot's CrossEncoder reranker runs in-request on CPU (BASE-QUAL-02), and torch will happily saturate every core; the unbounded SQLAlchemy pool (BASE-CONFIG-01) and unbounded Celery memory (no time limits, BASE-CONFIG-21) let a runaway task exhaust RAM. With no limits, any of those takes down Postgres and Caddy along with the backend, because they share the same memory. A single OOM kills the database rather than the offending worker.

Capabilities compound it: containers keep the full default set, so a container escape has more to work with than it needs. The backend image does at least run as a non-root user (backend/Dockerfile:23-24), which is the one hardening control present.
findings.remediation:
Add limits sized to the host, and drop what nothing uses:

    backend:
      mem_limit: 2g
      cpus: 2.0
      pids_limit: 200
      security_opt: ["no-new-privileges:true"]
      cap_drop: ["ALL"]

    db:
      mem_limit: 2g
      security_opt: ["no-new-privileges:true"]

    celery_worker:
      mem_limit: 3g      # torch + CrossEncoder need headroom
      cpus: 2.0

Leave db writable, but the frontend/nginx container can take `read_only: true` with tmpfs for /var/cache/nginx and /var/run. Set the numbers against the actual VPS size before deploying.

findings.title: Backups are written to the same host as the database and the schedule is documentation, not code
findings.vulnerable_code:
#   0 3 * * * cd /opt/uni-volunteer-scheduler && ./scripts/backup_db.sh >> backups/backup.log 2>&1
...
BACKUP_DIR="${BACKUP_DIR:-./backups}"
...
docker compose -f "${COMPOSE_FILE}" exec -T db \
  pg_dump -U "${DB_USER}" --no-owner "${DB_NAME}" | gzip > "${OUT}"
...
find "${BACKUP_DIR}" -name 'uvs-*.sql.gz' -mtime "+${RETENTION_DAYS}" -delete
findings.attack_scenario:
The script itself is well built — `set -euo pipefail`, an explicit empty-dump check, retention pruning, and a documented restore drill. Two things around it are not.

First, dumps land in ./backups on the same VPS as the Postgres volume they protect. That covers "someone dropped a table" and covers nothing else: host disk failure, a wiped or ransomwared VPS, or an accidental `docker compose down -v` destroys the database and all 14 days of backups together. There is no offsite copy step anywhere in the repo.

Second, the cron entry exists only as a comment on line 9. Nothing in docker-compose.prod.yml or any deploy script installs it, so on a fresh deployment following the compose file's own usage instructions, no backup ever runs. The failure is silent — you discover it when you need a restore.

Compounding: migration 0009 unconditionally deletes all signups (BASE-CONFIG-13), which is exactly the event a backup would need to cover.
findings.remediation:
Add an offsite push after the integrity check and before pruning:

    aws s3 cp "${OUT}" "s3://${BACKUP_BUCKET}/uvs/" --storage-class STANDARD_IA
    # or: rclone copy "${OUT}" "${RCLONE_REMOTE}:uvs/"

and fail the script if it does not land, so a broken offsite copy is loud.

Install the schedule as part of deployment rather than leaving it in a comment — either a documented `crontab -l | { cat; echo "0 3 * * * ..."; } | crontab -` step in the runbook, or an ofelia/cron sidecar service in docker-compose.prod.yml. Then do the restore drill in the header at least once, against a scratch database, and record the date.

findings.title: The production backend image is single-stage and ships its compiler toolchain
findings.exact_lines: 11, 18; no HEALTHCHECK instruction in the file
findings.vulnerable_code:
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y build-essential procps && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# Install Python deps
COPY requirements.txt /app/requirements.txt
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r /app/requirements.txt

# Copy backend source
COPY . /app
findings.attack_scenario:
build-essential is installed to compile wheels and then never removed, so gcc, make, and the C toolchain ship to production inside the running image. That is both image bloat and post-exploitation convenience: an attacker with code execution in the container has a compiler on hand.

`COPY . /app` copies the entire backend directory. Whether that includes a real .env depends on backend/.dockerignore — worth confirming directly, because if it does, secrets are baked into an image layer and survive in the layer cache even if the file is deleted in a later step.

The image also declares no HEALTHCHECK; the compose file supplies one for the backend service (docker-compose.prod.yml:81-86), so anything running this image outside that compose file has no liveness signal. Both are Low: the image already runs as a non-root user (line 23-24), which is the control that matters most here.
findings.remediation:
Split the build so the toolchain stays out of the runtime image:

    FROM python:3.10-slim AS build
    RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y build-essential && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
    COPY requirements.txt .
    RUN pip wheel --no-cache-dir --wheel-dir /wheels -r requirements.txt

    FROM python:3.10-slim
    RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y procps && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
    COPY --from=build /wheels /wheels
    RUN pip install --no-cache-dir /wheels/* && rm -rf /wheels

and verify backend/.dockerignore excludes .env, .env.*, tests/, and .git before the next build.

findings.title: POST /auth/token authenticated deactivated and soft-deleted staff, so offboarding could be undone by simply logging in again
findings.attack_scenario:
Found while fixing BASE-SEC-01, not by the original sweep. The login handler checked that the user exists and that the password verifies, and then minted a token — it never consulted is_active or deleted_at.

So deactivating a staff account did not merely fail to invalidate their existing session (BASE-SEC-01); it failed to stop them obtaining a brand new one. A departed organizer who still knew their password could log in the day after being offboarded and would receive a fully valid access token plus a 14-day refresh token. The admin UI would show them as inactive throughout.

Because the account also remained absent from the deactivation checks on the refresh path, there was no layer at which offboarding actually took effect.
findings.remediation: FIXED 2026-08-09. The handler now calls _account_usable(user) after password verification and returns the same "Incorrect email or password" detail as a wrong password, so the endpoint does not become an oracle for which accounts exist or have been disabled. Regression test: test_deactivated_user_cannot_log_back_in.

findings.title: No .dockerignore anywhere: backend/.env (JWT signing secret, SendGrid key, Twilio credentials) is baked into every backend image layer
findings.vulnerable_code: COPY . /app
findings.attack_scenario: VERIFIED by orchestrator: `ls backend/.dockerignore frontend/.dockerignore .dockerignore` -> all three No such file or directory. `backend/.env` exists on disk (1484 bytes) and contains DATABASE_URL, JWT_SECRET, SENDGRID_API_KEY, TWILIO_ACCOUNT_SID, TWILIO_AUTH_TOKEN. backend/Dockerfile:18 is `COPY . /app` and the build context is ./backend (docker-compose.yml:40-41, docker-compose.prod.yml:63-64). .gitignore excludes .env from git, but Docker does not consult .gitignore -- the live secrets are therefore written into an immutable image layer shared by the backend, migrate, celery_worker and celery_beat containers. Anyone who can pull the image, `docker save` it, read the registry, or exec into any of those four containers recovers JWT_SECRET, which under HS256 (app/deps.py:115) yields forged admin tokens for any account. Layer history preserves the file even if a later layer deletes it. The same COPY also ships backend/.venv/, .coverage, .pytest_cache/, .ruff_cache/, __pycache__/ and the whole tests/ tree into the production runtime. Distinct from BASE-CONFIG-19 (a literal in ci.yml); this is the build-packaging path.
findings.remediation: Add backend/.dockerignore with at minimum: .env, .env.*, !.env.production.example, .venv/, .coverage, .pytest_cache/, .ruff_cache/, __pycache__/, tests/, .DS_Store. Add frontend/.dockerignore with node_modules/, dist/, .env*. Then ROTATE JWT_SECRET, SENDGRID_API_KEY and the Twilio credentials, because any image already built from this context contains them -- rotating is the remediation, the .dockerignore only stops recurrence. The env_file: directives in both compose files already inject these at runtime, so nothing depends on the file being inside the image.
findings.remediation_applied: Same fix as BASE-SEC-02. Secret rotation still outstanding.

findings.title: requirements.txt is a partial pin, not a lockfile: torch/sentence-transformers/openai transitives are unconstrained at build time
findings.vulnerable_code:
openai>=1.30.0
pgvector>=0.3,<1.0
sentence-transformers>=3.0,<4
torch>=2.2,<3
numpy>=1.26,<2
tiktoken>=0.6,<1
sentry-sdk>=2.0,<3
findings.attack_scenario: VERIFIED: no Python lockfile exists anywhere in the repo (no pyproject.toml, no poetry.lock, no uv.lock, no *.lock under backend/, no --hash= entries). Lines 7-80 are hand-frozen exact pins; lines 81-87 are open ranges, and the packages those pull -- transformers, huggingface-hub, tokenizers, safetensors, requests, urllib3, certifi, jinja2, scipy, scikit-learn, sympy, networkx, tqdm, httpcore -- appear nowhere in the file and are resolved fresh on every `docker build` (backend/Dockerfile:15) and every CI run (.github/workflows/ci.yml:63). Two consequences: (1) the image that was tested is not the image that ships, and a rebuild months later silently changes the dependency set; (2) transitive advisories cannot even be assessed -- `transformers` carries GHSA-29pf-2h5f-8g72 (RCE) and GHSA-fgcw-684q-jj6r (arbitrary code execution during model init), and because no version is recorded it is impossible to state whether the deployed image is inside or outside those ranges. That unknowability IS the finding. `openai>=1.30.0` additionally has no upper bound at all.
findings.remediation: Generate a fully-resolved hash-pinned lockfile (`pip-compile --generate-hashes` or `uv pip compile --generate-hashes`) and install with `pip install --require-hashes`. Add an upper bound to openai (>=1.30,<2). Caveat: --require-hashes is incompatible with the unpinned --extra-index-url torch resolution as currently written (see BASE-CONFIG-34), so the CPU torch wheel must be pinned to an exact version+hash from download.pytorch.org in the same change. Budget one build iteration for the CPU-wheel hashes.

findings.title: pip --extra-index-url is not package-scoped, exposing all ~87 backend packages to index substitution
findings.vulnerable_code: --extra-index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu
findings.attack_scenario: VERIFIED present at line 6. pip does not scope an extra index to particular packages: for every requirement it queries BOTH PyPI and download.pytorch.org and installs the highest version found on either. pip's own documentation names this class of issue (dependency confusion) and states the option is unsafe. If the PyTorch wheel index were ever compromised or made to serve a file named e.g. `celery-99.0.0`, pip would prefer it over the PyPI pin and execute attacker code inside `docker build` (backend/Dockerfile:15) and inside the CI runner (.github/workflows/ci.yml:63). Blast radius is every container built from ./backend. No hash pinning exists to contain it (BASE-CONFIG-33).
findings.remediation: Split the install: keep PyPI as the only index for requirements.txt, and install the CPU torch wheel in a separate explicitly-scoped step -- `RUN pip install --no-cache-dir --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu torch==<exact>` BEFORE `RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt`. Ordering matters: installing requirements.txt first pulls the CUDA torch build from PyPI, which is the ~2GB problem the comment at lines 2-5 exists to avoid. Alternatively adopt --require-hashes so a substituted artifact fails checksum.

findings.title: python-multipart 0.0.20: seven advisories including two HIGH parser DoS, on the unauthenticated login form path
findings.vulnerable_code: python-multipart==0.0.20
findings.attack_scenario: VERIFIED pin at line 59. python-multipart is the form parser Starlette/FastAPI dispatch to, and backend/app/routers/auth.py:307 takes `form_data: OAuth2PasswordRequestForm = Depends()` on the unauthenticated login route -- a pre-auth attacker reaches the parser directly. Advisories matching 0.0.20: GHSA-pp6c-gr5w-3c5g (HIGH, DoS via unbounded multipart part headers, <0.0.27); GHSA-5rvq-cxj2-64vf (HIGH, quadratic-time querystring parsing with semicolon separators, <0.0.30); GHSA-wp53-j4wj-2cfg (HIGH, arbitrary file write, <0.0.22, requires a non-default config this app does not use); GHSA-mj87-hwqh-73pj (large preamble/epilogue DoS, <0.0.26); plus GHSA-v9pg-7xvm-68hf, GHSA-6jv3-5f52-599m and GHSA-vffw-93wf-4j4q. Practical impact: an unauthenticated POST to /api/v1/auth/token with unbounded part headers or a semicolon-dense body pegs a uvicorn worker's event loop; with only 4 workers (docker-compose.prod.yml:80) the whole API stalls.
findings.remediation:
Move to python-multipart==0.0.31 or later, which clears every range above. The repo does not import it directly (it is consumed through Starlette), so the upgrade is drop-in; re-run the auth tests to confirm OAuth2PasswordRequestForm still parses.

--- FIXED 2026-08-12. python-multipart bumped 0.0.20 -> 0.0.32 in backend/requirements.txt, clearing all seven advisories. This half was independent of BASE-CONFIG-36 despite the shared remediation note.

findings.title: starlette 0.50.0: request.form() limits silently ignored for urlencoded bodies (HIGH, CVSS 7.5), on the unauthenticated login route
findings.vulnerable_code: starlette==0.50.0
findings.attack_scenario: VERIFIED pin at line 67. GHSA-82w8-qh3p-5jfq / CVE-2026-54283, HIGH (7.5): 'request.form() limits silently ignored for application/x-www-form-urlencoded enable DoS', affected >=0.4.1 <1.3.1, patched 1.3.1. The advisory states FastAPI applications are affected. POST /api/v1/auth/token (auth.py:307, OAuth2PasswordRequestForm) is an unauthenticated application/x-www-form-urlencoded endpoint -- precisely the affected content type. A sub-10MB body with ~1M fields blocks the asyncio event loop for seconds per request; docker-compose.prod.yml:80 runs `--workers 4`, so a handful of concurrent requests takes the API offline. The Redis rate limiter (app/deps.py:42-74) does not help: the parse happens inside the handler, and the limiter is keyed on request.client.host, which BASE-CONFIG-27 already shows is attacker-controlled because the backend runs --forwarded-allow-ips=*.
findings.remediation:
Upgrade starlette to >=1.3.1. BREAKING: fastapi==0.123.5 declares `starlette<0.51.0,>=0.40.0`, so starlette cannot move alone -- fastapi must move to a release whose constraint allows it. Treat as a coordinated fastapi+starlette major bump with a full pytest + Playwright pass, not a point upgrade. Interim mitigation that is safe to ship immediately: bound request body size at the Caddy edge with `request_body { max_size 1MB }`.

--- MITIGATED 2026-08-12, still open. The proper fix is starlette >= 1.3.1 and it cannot be pinned here: fastapi 0.123.5 requires starlette < 0.51.0, and the fastapi that permits starlette 1.x (0.141.1) hangs the backend suite indefinitely at tests/copilot/agent/test_confirm_authorization.py::test_owner_can_still_confirm (13 minutes against a 4-minute baseline, killed). Verified by running it, not assumed. Both pins were reverted. The ceiling now lives at the edge instead, where it does not depend on the framework honouring anything: Caddyfile declares request_body { max_size 2MB }, well above any legitimate request this app makes. Two limits on that mitigation, recorded deliberately: it only protects traffic that arrives through Caddy, so the backend port must never be published separately, and it does not fix the library. Re-attempt the bump when the fastapi hang is diagnosed.

findings.title: starlette 0.50.0: Host-header poisoning of request.url.path, which this app uses for both its CSP exemption and its rate-limit key
findings.vulnerable_code: starlette==0.50.0
findings.attack_scenario: GHSA-86qp-5c8j-p5mr / CVE-2026-48710, MODERATE (6.5): missing Host header validation poisons request.url.path, bypassing path-based security checks; affected <=1.0.0, patched 1.0.1. This app makes two security decisions from request.url.path, both orchestrator-verified: backend/app/main.py:96 skips the `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'` header when the path starts with /docs, /redoc or /openapi.json; and backend/app/deps.py:58 builds the rate-limit bucket as `f"rate:{request.client.host}:{request.url.path}"`. A crafted `Host: example.com/docs?x=` re-parses the URL so request.url.path reads /docs regardless of the real target, which (a) strips CSP off every API JSON response and (b) splits or collapses rate-limit buckets, letting an attacker spread login attempts across synthetic keys and evade the per-endpoint throttle. Also matching this pin: GHSA-jp82-jpqv-5vv3 (LOW, path not starting with '/' poisons request.url.hostname, <1.3.0).
findings.remediation: Covered by the same coordinated fastapi+starlette bump as BASE-CONFIG-36 (>=1.3.1 clears both). Defence-in-depth that is safe to apply immediately and independently of the bump: key the rate limiter and the CSP exemption off `request.scope['path']` (the raw ASGI path, not derived from Host) instead of request.url.path, and add Starlette's TrustedHostMiddleware pinned to $DOMAIN in backend/app/main.py.

findings.title: Authlib 1.6.5: Critical signature-verification bypass chain on dead-but-present SSO routes
findings.vulnerable_code: Authlib==1.6.5
findings.attack_scenario: SEVERITY CORRECTED by orchestrator from the subagent's High to Medium, on verified evidence of unreachability. The advisories are real: GHSA-wvwj-cvrp-7pv5 / CVE-2026-27962 'JWS JWK Header Injection: Signature Verification Bypass', CRITICAL CVSS 9.1, affected 0.1 through 1.6.8, fixed 1.6.9 (confirmed directly against api.osv.dev by the orchestrator); plus GHSA-7wc2-qxgw-g8gg (alg:none with blank signature), GHSA-m344-f55w-2m6j (fail-open OIDC hash binding), GHSA-7432-952r-cw78 (JWE RSA1_5 Bleichenbacher oracle), GHSA-fg6f-75jq-6523 (1-click account takeover), GHSA-w8p2-r796-3vmq and GHSA-r95x-qfjj-fjj2 (open redirects), GHSA-jj8c-mmj3-mmgv (CSRF). backend/app/routers/auth.py:10 does import OAuth, and /auth/sso/login and /auth/sso/callback do exist (auth.py:388-425), where sso_callback auto-registers and logs in the asserted identity and mints a first-party access token -- so IF the flow were live this would be a full authentication bypass. It is NOT live: auth.py:132 registers university_sso only `if settings.oidc_client_id and settings.oidc_client_secret and settings.oidc_issuer`, all four OIDC_* keys in backend/.env are present-but-EMPTY, backend/.env.production.example defines no OIDC keys at all, and config.py:39-41 defaults them to None. Both routes short-circuit on `if "university_sso" not in oauth`. The finding is therefore latent: it becomes Critical the moment anyone populates the OIDC settings.
findings.remediation: Preferred: delete the two /sso/* routes, the `from authlib...` import at auth.py:10, the oauth.register block at auth.py:132-137 and the Authlib pin. The product pivoted to account-less signup with magic links (see docs and the v1.1 realignment), so this is dead code carrying a Critical CVE. If SSO is genuinely on the roadmap, upgrade to a release past every range above (>=1.6.12; confirm the current release at fix time) and smoke-test authorize_access_token() against the real IdP, since the 1.7.x line tightened JWS/JWT algorithm handling. Either way, do not enable OIDC on 1.6.5.

findings.title: Every base image pinned to a mutable tag, none by digest; Python 3.10 reaches end-of-life October 2026
findings.vulnerable_code: image: pgvector/pgvector:pg16
findings.attack_scenario: Six base images, zero digests: pgvector/pgvector:pg16 (docker-compose.yml:3, prod:23), redis:7 (dev:18, prod:38), caddy:2 (prod:144), axllent/mailpit:latest (dev:28 -- a floating `latest`), python:3.10-slim (backend/Dockerfile:2, orchestrator-verified), node:20-alpine and nginx:1.27-alpine (frontend/Dockerfile:11,25). Mutable tags mean two `docker compose up --build` runs a week apart produce different images with no record of the difference -- the deployed artifact is unauditable -- and a hijacked upstream tag is pulled silently on the next restart, which `restart: unless-stopped` on every service makes routine. pgvector/pgvector is a community image, not a Docker Official Image, widening that trust boundary. Separately, Python 3.10 is in security-fix-only status with EOL scheduled October 2026, roughly two months after this audit, after which the interpreter gets no fixes and the slim image stops being rebuilt.
findings.remediation: Pin each image by digest (`image: pgvector/pgvector:pg16@sha256:<digest>`, `FROM python:3.10-slim@sha256:<digest>`) and update digests through reviewed PRs; a Dependabot `docker` ecosystem entry automates the churn. Replace axllent/mailpit:latest with an explicit version even though it is dev-only. Separately plan the move to python:3.12-slim before October 2026 -- SQLAlchemy 2.0.44, celery 5.6.0 and torch all support 3.12, but verify the alembic slug-revision workaround in alembic/env.py and C-extension wheel availability on the target interpreter first.

findings.title: CI: GitHub Actions pinned to mutable major tags, no permissions block, no dependency-audit step, no Dependabot
findings.vulnerable_code: - uses: actions/checkout@v4
findings.attack_scenario: All six action references use floating major tags: actions/checkout@v4 (lines 54, 187, 210), actions/setup-python@v5 (55, 217), actions/setup-node@v4 (188, 211), actions/upload-artifact@v4 (280). A major tag is a mutable git ref -- whoever controls the action repository, or an attacker who compromises it, can repoint v4 at arbitrary code running inside the runner with GITHUB_TOKEN and the npm/pip caches. Mitigating: all four are first-party GitHub-maintained actions and the workflow uses no third-party actions, which is the single biggest thing this CI gets right. Compounding: no top-level or job-level `permissions:` block, so GITHUB_TOKEN takes the repository default for jobs that need only `contents: read`; and the workflow runs on pull_request with `docker compose up` and `npm ci` over fork-authored lockfiles. There is no pip-audit/npm audit step and no .github/dependabot.yml -- which is precisely why BASE-CONFIG-35/36/38 went unnoticed through several release cycles.
findings.remediation: Pin each action to a full 40-character commit SHA with the tag in a trailing comment. Add `permissions: contents: read` at the top of the workflow, granting more only to the job that needs it. Add .github/dependabot.yml covering pip, npm, docker and github-actions. Add a non-blocking `pip-audit -r backend/requirements.txt` and `npm audit --audit-level=high` step so new advisories surface on the PR rather than in an audit a year later.

findings.title: passlib 1.7.4 is unmaintained since October 2020 and is the password-hashing primitive for every staff account
findings.vulnerable_code: passlib==1.7.4
findings.attack_scenario: No advisory currently matches passlib 1.7.4 -- this is a maintenance-posture finding, not a CVE. 1.7.4 shipped 8 October 2020 and is still the latest release: five years and ten months with no release as of this audit. passlib is not peripheral: backend/app/deps.py:29-32 builds the CryptContext and deps.py:81-95 is the only password hashing/verification path (PBKDF2-SHA256), covering every admin and organizer credential. An unmaintained crypto library means any future parameter-strength deprecation, timing issue or Python-version incompatibility gets no upstream fix. passlib 1.7.4 is also known to break against newer bcrypt releases, and bcrypt==5.0.0 is pinned at line 15 -- a live compatibility cliff rather than a theoretical one.
findings.remediation: Migrate the CryptContext in backend/app/deps.py to a maintained primitive -- argon2-cffi (Argon2id) or the bcrypt package used directly (already a dependency). Caveat: existing stored hashes are PBKDF2-SHA256 and cannot be converted offline. Implement transparent rehash-on-successful-login (verify against the legacy scheme, then re-store under the new one) and keep passlib installed for the deprecation window. Do not attempt a same-release swap -- it would lock out every existing account.

findings.title: python-jose 3.5.0: no current advisories, but a thin-maintenance JOSE library with demonstrated multi-year patch latency on the core token path
findings.vulnerable_code: python-jose==3.5.0
findings.attack_scenario: Advisory check: the four python-jose advisories are GHSA-6c5p-j8vq-pqhj / CVE-2024-33663 (algorithm confusion, Critical), GHSA-cjwg-qfpm-7377 / CVE-2024-33664 (JWE decompression DoS), GHSA-w799-prg3-cx77 / CVE-2016-7036, and GHSA-h4pw-wxh7-4vjj (withdrawn Dec 2025). NONE matches 3.5.0 -- the 2024 pair were fixed in 3.4.0. The finding is the risk profile, not a live CVE: release cadence runs 3.2.0 (Jul 2020) -> 3.3.0 (Jun 2021) -> 3.4.0 (Feb 2025), a 3.7-year gap during which those two advisories sat unpatched, on a library carrying this app's entire authentication surface (app/deps.py:115/150/186 sign and verify access tokens; services/invite.py and services/password_reset.py mint and verify magic-link tokens). It also drags in ecdsa and rsa, adding the attack surface behind BASE-CONFIG-44 and BASE-CONFIG-45 that the HS256 configuration never uses.
findings.remediation: No upgrade is available or needed today -- 3.5.0 is current and clean. Plan a migration to PyJWT or joserfc; the call sites are five jwt.encode/jwt.decode pairs and PyJWT's signature is near-identical for HS256. Caveat: PyJWT raises its own exception types, so the `from jose import JWTError, ExpiredSignatureError` handling at auth.py:161 and the try/except blocks in deps.py, invite.py and password_reset.py all need rewriting. Migrating also drops the ecdsa and rsa transitives, retiring BASE-CONFIG-44 and BASE-CONFIG-45.

findings.title: cryptography 46.0.3: seven advisories match the pin, including a vulnerable statically-linked OpenSSL in the wheel
findings.vulnerable_code: cryptography==46.0.3
findings.attack_scenario: Seven GHSAs match this exact pin: GHSA-537c-gmf6-5ccf (HIGH 7.5, vulnerable OpenSSL statically linked into the wheel, out-of-bounds read, <48.0.1); GHSA-jwv3-5hgf-82ww (HIGH 8.7, exponential X.509 path-building, <=48.0.0); GHSA-g6cj-pr64-35w5 (HIGH 8.2, PKCS#7 EnvelopedData Bleichenbacher oracle, <50.0.0); GHSA-r6ph-v2qm-q3c2 (HIGH, missing subgroup validation for SECT curves, <46.0.5); GHSA-p423-j2cm-9vmq (MODERATE, buffer overflow with non-contiguous buffers, <46.0.7); GHSA-m2h6-j472-rp4c (MODERATE, wildcard DNS escape from permittedSubtrees); GHSA-m959-cc7f-wv43 (LOW, incomplete DNS name-constraint enforcement). Severity is Low HERE rather than at raw CVSS: the app configures HS256 only (config.py:14, .env.production.example:12), so no ECDSA/SECT curve, no RSA decryption and no PKCS#7 EnvelopedData path is exercised; it builds no X.509 chains and runs no custom certificate verifier, since TLS termination is Caddy's using Go's stdlib. The bundled-OpenSSL OOB read is the only one with any plausible reach, and only through cryptography's own primitives.
findings.remediation: Move to cryptography==50.0.0 (confirmed current on PyPI by the orchestrator), the only version past every range above including the <50.0.0 PKCS#7 range. Caveat: the repo does not import cryptography directly -- it is a transitive of python-jose and Authlib -- so verify only that those two still resolve against it.

findings.title: ecdsa 0.19.1: DER parsing DoS (fixed) plus an unfixable Minerva timing side channel; unreachable under HS256
findings.attack_scenario: GHSA-9f5j-8jwj-x28g / CVE-2026-33936, MODERATE (5.3): DoS via improper DER length validation in crafted private keys, affected <0.19.2. Low here because the vector requires the application to parse attacker-supplied DER private keys via SigningKey.from_der(); ecdsa reaches this app only as a python-jose transitive, and grep across backend/app finds no from_der/from_pem call and no ECDSA key material -- token signing is HS256/HMAC (config.py:14, deps.py:115-118). Also matching the pin: GHSA-wj6h-64fc-37mp / CVE-2024-23342, the Minerva timing attack on P-256, HIGH (7.4), affecting ALL versions with NO patch available -- the maintainers state side-channel attacks are out of scope with no planned fix. That one cannot be remediated by upgrading, only by removing the dependency; it is unreachable here for the same HS256 reason, since it requires SigningKey.sign_digest() on P-256.
findings.remediation: Bump to ecdsa==0.19.2 to clear CVE-2026-33936. There is no fix at any version for CVE-2024-23342 -- the only real remediation is to eliminate ecdsa from the tree, which happens automatically if the python-jose -> PyJWT migration in BASE-CONFIG-42 is carried out. Because ecdsa is a transitive, pinning it explicitly is what makes the 0.19.2 bump stick.

findings.title: pyasn1 0.6.1: five decoder denial-of-service advisories, all fixed upstream; unreachable under HS256
findings.attack_scenario: Five advisories match: GHSA-63vm-454h-vhhq (HIGH, decoder DoS, >=0.6.1 <0.6.2 -- the pin is the first affected release); GHSA-jr27-m4p2-rc6r (HIGH, unbounded recursion, <0.6.3); GHSA-m4p7-r5rc-7g4j (HIGH, BER/CER/DER decoder DoS via unbounded long-form tag IDs, <0.6.4); GHSA-8ppf-4f7h-5ppj (HIGH, quadratic complexity in OBJECT IDENTIFIER / RELATIVE-OID processing, <0.6.4); GHSA-hm4w-wwcw-mr6r (HIGH, uncontrolled resource consumption converting decoded REAL values, <0.6.4). Low in this application because every one requires feeding attacker-controlled ASN.1/DER into the decoder, and pyasn1 arrives only under rsa -> python-jose, which the HS256 configuration never invokes; no route accepts certificates, DER keys, or SNMP/LDAP payloads. RE-SCORE TO MEDIUM if the OIDC/SSO path in BASE-CONFIG-38 is ever enabled with an RS256 IdP -- the JWKS fetch would then feed remote key material through the ASN.1 stack.
findings.remediation: Pin pyasn1==0.6.4, which clears all five ranges. It is currently an implicit transitive; the explicit bump is safe and non-breaking, as pyasn1 0.6.x is API-stable within the series.

findings.title: idna 3.11: encode() bypass of the CVE-2024-3651 fix, on the untrusted volunteer-signup email path
findings.vulnerable_code: idna==3.11
findings.attack_scenario: GHSA-65pc-fj4g-8rjx / CVE-2026-45409, MODERATE: specially crafted inputs to idna.encode() bypass the CVE-2024-3651 fix; affected <3.15, patched 3.15. Reachable with genuinely untrusted input: email-validator==2.3.0 (line 28) normalises the domain part of every address submitted through the account-less volunteer signup flow and calls idna.encode() to do so; httpx also routes outbound hostnames through it. Rated Low rather than Medium because the signup route is rate-limited (app/deps.py:42-74) and the amplification factor is far smaller than BASE-CONFIG-36, which dominates the same threat.
findings.remediation: Bump to idna>=3.15 (3.18 is current). Drop-in, no API change -- idna is a pure-Python transitive of email-validator, httpx and requests.

findings.title: Werkzeug 3.1.4 pinned into the production image but imported nowhere
findings.vulnerable_code: Werkzeug==3.1.4
findings.attack_scenario: VERIFIED by orchestrator: `grep -rn werkzeug backend/app backend/tests` returns zero matches. This is a Flask-era leftover in a FastAPI/Starlette application, yet it is installed into all four backend containers. It carries GHSA-29vq-49wr-vm6x / CVE-2026-27199 and GHSA-87hc-h4r5-73f7 / CVE-2026-21860, both MODERATE, safe_join() allowing Windows special device names. Confirm with a clean `pip install -r requirements.txt` in a scratch container followed by `pytest -q` -- if nothing pulls it transitively and the suite passes, it was genuinely dead. click==8.3.1
pytest==8.3.3
python-dotenv==1.2.1
pydantic-settings==2.12.0

findings.title: react-router 7.14.0: open redirect reachable from client-side navigation in the shipped SPA
findings.vulnerable_code: "react-router-dom": "^7.11.0",
findings.attack_scenario: VERIFIED by orchestrator: package-lock.json resolves react-router and react-router-dom to 7.14.0; the caret range does not pin. Two advisories apply to the client-side (BrowserRouter, non-SSR) usage in frontend/src/main.jsx: GHSA-wrjc-x8rr-h8h6 / CVE-2026-53669, open redirect via backslash in <Link> and useNavigate, affected >=6.0.0 <7.18.0; and GHSA-2j2x-hqr9-3h42 / CVE-2026-40181, same-origin redirect with a path starting `//` reinterpreted as a protocol-relative URL, affected >=7.0.0 <7.14.1. Exploit path in this app: the magic-link and signup-confirmation flows land users on the SPA and navigate onward, so anywhere a redirect target comes from a query parameter or an API response, a value like `\\evil.com` or `//evil.com` navigates the volunteer off-site while the URL still looks like the SciTrek domain -- a credible phishing pivot for a system whose entire auth model is emailed magic links. GHSA-chx6-hx7r-mcp5 (unauthenticated DoS via inefficient route matching, <7.18.0) also matches but is client-side-only here, burning the visitor's own CPU, so it does not raise the severity.
findings.remediation: Move react-router-dom to ^7.18.0, which clears every 7.x range including the SSR-only ones. Caveat: 7.15-7.18 introduced RSC/framework-mode APIs, but the data-router and BrowserRouter APIs this app uses are stable across the range; re-run `npm run test -- --run` and the Playwright suite. Do this in its own PR, separate from the vitest bump in BASE-CONFIG-51.

findings.title: Frontend dev toolchain carries a Critical (vitest UI file read/execute) plus nested duplicate copies of vite and esbuild
findings.attack_scenario: Scanning all 454 lockfile entries returned ten vulnerable resolutions, ALL in the dev/test tree -- the top-level vite 7.3.2 resolution is clean. vitest@2.1.9 -> GHSA-5xrq-8626-4rwp / CVE-2026-47429, CRITICAL: when the Vitest UI server is listening, an arbitrary file can be read and executed, affected <3.2.6 (@vitest/ui is a declared devDependency). vitest 2.1.9 also drags in a second older bundler copy: vite@5.4.21 (orchestrator-verified in the lock at node_modules/vitest/node_modules/vite) -> GHSA-fx2h-pf6j-xcff and GHSA-4w7w-66w2-5vf9, server.fs.deny bypasses, dev-server only; and esbuild@0.21.5 -> GHSA-67mh-4wv8-2f99. Also postcss@8.5.9 -> GHSA-6g55-p6wh-862q (HIGH, arbitrary file read via attacker-controlled sourceMappingURL); js-yaml@4.1.1 (HIGH, quadratic CPU); ws@8.20.0 (HIGH); form-data@4.0.5 (HIGH, CRLF injection); brace-expansion@1.1.13; @babel/core@7.29.0.
